<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The European Union is currently facing a demographic, digital, and environmental transition collectively known as the triple transition. Although these trends significantly impact long-term care services, they have typically been studied in isolation, overlooking potential synergies between the adoption of digital tools and environmental practices among informal caregivers of older adults. This study uniquely bridges this gap by applying an integrative social-ecological-infrastructural systems framework to examine how these transitions interact in everyday caregiving contexts.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study examined the relationship between the use of digital tools and eco-friendly practices among informal caregivers of older adults across the European Union and whether the adoption of digital solutions related differently to specific types of eco-friendly behaviors. Unlike previous research focusing on isolated aspects of each transition, we examined their interconnections, providing empirical evidence for developing integrated policy approaches.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using data from the Survey of Gender Gaps in Unpaid Care, Individual and Social Activities project (n=5761 informal caregivers of adults aged ≥65 years), we analyzed the association between frequency of use of digital tools for caregiving and environmental practices. We used the social-ecological-infrastructural systems conceptual framework and the theory of planned behavior (TPB) to interpret findings. Analyses included descriptive statistics, Spearman correlations, and multilevel mixed-effects regression models.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      A weak positive association was observed between the frequency of use of digital tools and environmentally sustainable behaviors (ρ=0.28;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      <.001). Among individual behaviors, the largest associations were observed for consumption-related behaviors (fair-trade products: ρ=0.30; used items: ρ=0.30; eco-friendly products: ρ=0.25), whereas the associations were weaker for waste management and transportation choices and were not statistically significant for recycling (ρ=−0.04;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.23) and mindful consumption of natural resources (ρ=−0.02;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      >.99). Respondents using digital tools daily had scores of environmentally sustainable behavior (SESBs) 22% higher than nonusers. Demographic patterns revealed higher use of digital tools among younger, more educated, and employed caregivers, indicating that any potential digital-environmental co-occurrence may be unevenly distributed across the caregiver population.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The use of digital tools may be related to environmental behavior through improved access to information, peer norms, and a greater perceived ability to act, though these mechanisms were not directly tested. The stronger associations with consumption-related behaviors indicate that digital platforms may be particularly relevant to caregivers’ access to eco-friendly products, second-hand goods, fair-trade options, and sustainable local services. By contrast, the lack of statistically significant correlations with recycling and resource conservation suggests that digital solutions alone may be insufficient to address behaviors that depend on structural conditions, physical infrastructure, local service availability, or established household routines. Policies should consider digital inclusion, caregiver support, and green infrastructure as interconnected areas while ensuring that older, less educated, and more burdened caregivers are not excluded from these potential co-benefits.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Use of Digital Tools and Environmental Practices Among Informal Caregivers of Older Adults in the European Union Embracing the Triple Transition: Cross-Sectional Study

<jats:title>AbstractR</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Qualitative methods are foundational to gerontological research, yet conventional analytic approaches may obscure the relational, moral, and embodied dimensions of caregiving that unfold across aging care systems. Women of color employed in long-term care who also provide unpaid caregiving inhabit intersecting landscapes of care that remain under-described. This study responds to calls for methodological innovation in gerontology by advancing poetic inquiry as a rigorous qualitative approach for illuminating caregiving across institutional and domestic contexts.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Guided by feminist ethics and intersectionality, semi-structured interviews were conducted with eight women of color working in long-term care who also identified as family caregivers. Using a voice-centered relational approach, I-Poems were constructed from transcripts to preserve first-person language, temporal flow, and meaning. Grounded in the Listening Guide, analysis emphasized relational listening, reflexivity, and attentiveness to marginalized voices, positioning poems as both analytic products and ethical encounters.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The I-Poems illuminate caregiving as intersubjective, continuous, and morally grounded, characterized by blurred boundaries between paid and unpaid care, work and home, self and other, and obligation and choice. Care emerged not as discrete roles but as a way of being-with others across aging contexts.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings challenge work–life balance discourses and call for relationally attuned workplace policies that recognize caregiving as socially embedded and valued labor. By demonstrating poetic inquiry as a methodological and ethical innovation, this study expands analytic possibilities for research on caregiving and aging and is generative for future studies with underrepresented populations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Invisible labor, relational lives: Poetic inquiry into women of color navigating dual-role caregiving

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>As the mean age of the world’s population rises, there is increasing demand for long-term post-acute care (LTPAC), where health information technology (HIT) has potential to improve care quality, access, and equity. However, evidence guiding effective HIT implementation in LTPAC remains limited. Authors of this paper report on proceedings from the International Summit on Innovation and Technology in Care of Older People (IS-ITCOP) and present a consensus-driven policy-relevant research agenda to advance HIT use in LTPAC. A two-day international summit convened 47 experts in research, policy, clinical care, and technology. Plenary sessions with keynotes and facilitated discussion groups addressed four domains: emerging care models and technology, workforce of the future, transparency and accountability, and safety and privacy. Data from recordings, structured notes, and word cloud visualization were synthesized to identify consensus-based research priorities. Key priorities include developing equitable and interoperable technology-enabled care models; strengthening workforce readiness through digital competencies, informatics leadership, and training; redesigning accountability systems to reduce reporting burden and improve data validity; and addressing ethical, privacy, cybersecurity, and consent concerns. Cross-cutting themes highlighted infrastructure limitations, policy misalignment, workforce shortages, and disparities in technology access across settings. Advancing HIT in LTPAC requires coordinated policy, infrastructure, workforce, and governance strategies. Findings support the need for investment in interoperability, workforce development, equitable technology design, and person-centered implementation approaches to improve quality, safety, and outcomes for older adults receiving long-term care.</jats:p>
title: Health technology innovation in long-term care of older people: Advancing a policy-relevant research agenda

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Macroeconomic shocks may influence cognitive function in later life. We examined cognitive trajectories around the 2007-2009 Global Financial Crisis (GFC) among older Australians and whether resilience factors modified these trajectories.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We used longitudinal data from 1,872 community-dwelling adults in the 60-66-year cohort of the PATH Through Life Study. Participants were followed from 2001-2002 to 2020-2021 across six waves (∼4-year intervals). Perceived financial impact of the GFC and co-occurring distress/anxiety were assessed at wave 3 (2009-2010) and categorised as no impact, impact without distress/anxiety, and impact with distress/anxiety. A global cognitive composite was calculated and standardised as z-scores. Linear mixed-effects models estimated pre-GFC change, change during the GFC, and post-GFC change. Effect modification by 13 resilience factors was examined.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Most reported no financial impact (66.2%); 23.8% reported impact without distress/anxiety, and 10.0% with distress/anxiety. Pre-GFC cognitive decline was similar across groups. During the GFC, all groups experienced a decline (-0.057 to -0.091 SD). During the post-GFC period, cognition declined further at similar rates in the no impact, impact without distress/anxiety, and impact with distress/anxiety groups: -0.073 SD/year (95% CI: -0.080, -0.066), -0.070 (-0.079, -0.060), and -0.069 (-0.083, -0.056), respectively. Higher physical health-related quality of life attenuated the decline during the GFC, while greater life satisfaction and positive social support were associated with slower post-GFC decline.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Cognitive decline increased around the GFC period and continued thereafter, with no evidence that these changes differed by perceived financial impact or distress/anxiety. Causal attribution to the GFC is limited by the absence of an unexposed comparison group.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Cognitive trajectories before and after the Global Financial Crisis: a 20-year cohort study of older adults in Australia

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Population aging has made old-age financial preparation increasingly consequential, yet it is typically indexed by a single measure that does not distinguish among the forms it takes. Drawing on Conservation of Resources theory and the institutional and normative structure of retirement in Korea, we examined associations between within-person changes in financial preparation and two distinct dimensions of subjective well-being among pre-old-age Korean adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using seven biennial waves (2011–2023) of the Korean Retirement and Income Study (9,887 person-waves; 2,389 individuals), we estimated individual fixed-effects regressions examining associations between old-age financial preparation and depressive symptoms, measured using the Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale (CES-D), and life satisfaction, adjusting for key time-varying covariates.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Within-person transitions into preparation were associated with a 1.02-point lower CES-D score and a 0.11-point higher life-satisfaction score on a 5-point scale (both p &lt; .001). Adequate preparation showed stronger associations with well-being than inadequate preparation (CES-D: β = −1.24 vs. −0.90; life satisfaction: β = 0.16 vs. 0.09); associations were comparable across primary preparation methods. A dose–response asymmetry emerged: associations with depressive symptoms plateaued beyond one preparation method, whereas life satisfaction increased additively with diversification (β difference = 0.077, p &lt; .01).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Old-age financial preparation appears to function as a within-person psychosocial resource related to both evaluative and affective dimensions of well-being. These divergent patterns suggest that the scope and adequacy of preparation matter differently for depressive symptoms and global life evaluations, potentially informing pension policy and financial-planning interventions in aging societies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Preparing for the future, feeling better now: Old-age financial preparation and psychological well-being in pre-old-age Korean adults

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This longitudinal study examined the relationship between objective visual acuity and subjective vision over a six-month period. Specifically, it investigated the moderating role of internalized ageist attitudes in shaping how objective vision relates to perceived sensory vision difficulties over time.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A sample of 139 community-dwelling participants (M=70.25, SD=5.57) underwent objective vision assessments (distance and near visual acuity, and contrast sensitivity) and completed the Fraboni Scale of Ageism at baseline (T1). Subjective vision assessments were conducted at T1 and six months later (T2). Hierarchical regression analyses were used to predict T2 subjective vision, controlling for baseline subjective vision, age, sex, relationship status, and self-rated health.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>No direct main effect of T1 objective vision on T2 subjective vision was found. However, higher baseline ageist attitudes significantly predicted poorer subjective vision at T2 (β=.14, p=.041). Crucially, a significant interaction emerged (β=.16, p=.018); objective vision at T1 predicted poorer subjective vision at T2 only among individuals with high levels of ageist attitudes. For those with low ageist attitudes, this association was non-significant.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings support Stereotype Embodiment Theory, suggesting that internalized ageist stereotypes asct as a cognitive lens through which individuals interpret biological sensory cues. The results indicate that subjective vision is not merely a reflection of physical decline but is significantly shaped by psychological frameworks. Clinical interventions aimed at reducing internalized ageist attitudes may mitigate the negative subjective experience of vision loss, potentially reducing functional vulnerabilities and enhancing overall well-being.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Ageist attitudes as a moderator of objective and subjective vision: A longitudinal study

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Understanding changes in long-term care (LTC) applicants’ needs informs service planning.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To examine trends in functional impairment and multimorbidity among Hong Kong’s publicly funded LTC applicants during 2001–2019.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We analyzed interRAI assessments from 315,556 applicants aged ≥60. Hierarchical mixed-effects models estimated trends in physical and cognitive impairment, loneliness, and multimorbidity, adjusting for age, birth cohort, and sociodemographic factors. Subgroup analyses examined differences by age, disease, and living status.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Cognitive impairment and multimorbidity increased, physical impairment plateaued, and loneliness declined. Stroke was associated with greater physical and cognitive impairment, and cataract with greater loneliness. Applicants aged ≥85 had more functional impairments but less multimorbidity.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Applicants’ functional and health needs became more complex and varied over time, differing by age, living arrangements, and disease profiles. These findings support integrated, tailored strategies to address changing health and social needs of older adults applying for publicly funded LTC services.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Older Adults Seeking Publicly Funded Long-Term Care in a Super-ageing Society: Trends in Functional Impairments and Multimorbidity Burden Based on InterRAI-Home Care Data From 2001 to 2019 in Hong Kong

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We use person-environment (PE) fit theory to examine whether neighborhood composition is associated with behavioral symptoms of cognitive decline among older Mexican Americans and their caregivers’ distress.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      We estimated multilevel regression models using 2011/2012 data from the Hispanic Established Population for the Epidemiological Study of the Elderly (
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">n</jats:italic>
                      = 862) linked to 2010 census tract characteristics (percent foreign born, Hispanic, and poor) from the National Neighborhood Data Archive, adjusting for care recipient and caregiver covariates.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Residing in areas with a higher proportion of foreign-born adults was associated with fewer neuropsychiatric symptoms, particularly delusions, agitation/aggression, depression/dysphoria, and anxiety, and with lower symptom severity. Higher tract poverty was marginally associated with greater odds of aberrant motor behavior, while tract characteristics were unrelated to caregiver distress.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Findings support a PE-fit interpretation in which immigrant enclaves, rather than Hispanic concentration, may influence behavioral symptom expression or their perceptions/reporting by caregivers.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Neighborhood Characteristics, Behavioral Symptoms of Cognitive Decline, and Caregivers’ Distress in Older Mexican Americans

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Hispanic individuals are understudied in cognitive aging research and are disproportionately exposed to crime, yet the cognitive consequences of this exposure remain unclear. We examined whether county-level crime moderates the association between physical functioning (PF) and cognitive change among Mexican Americans aged 75 years and older without cognitive impairment at baseline.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Participants included 1,189 older adults from the Hispanic Established Populations for the Epidemiologic Study of the Elderly (HEPESE). Cognitive functioning was measured using the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE), PF was assessed using performance-based measures, and total crime was measured at the county level. Multilevel models adjusted for demographic, socioeconomic, and cardiovascular factors.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Better PF was associated with higher MMSE scores. A significant interaction among PF, crime, and time indicated that the protective association between PF and cognitive functioning weakened as county-level crime increased. Higher PF predicted less cognitive decline in low- and moderate-crime areas, although this association was attenuated in moderate-crime contexts and largely absent in high-crime areas.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>County-level crime may undermine the cognitive benefits of better PF in late life. These findings underscore the role of contextual factors in cognitive aging among older Mexican Americans and highlight potential targets for community-level prevention efforts.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Physical Functioning, Crime, and Cognitive Decline in Mexican Americans: A Multi-Level Analysis of Protective Interactions

                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Neighborhood resources are protective factors for healthy cognitive aging, yet the impact of these resources may vary by urbanicity. We examined urban-rural differences in the association between the availability of neighborhood social services, religious, and civic organizations, and cognitive decline among older Mexican Americans.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Data from 628 participants (
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">M</jats:italic>
                      <jats:sub>Age</jats:sub>
                      = 80) in 2004–2013 Hispanic Established Populations for the Epidemiologic Study of the Elderly were linked to the National Neighborhood Data Archive. Cognitive impairment was measured with the Mini-Mental State Examination.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Among urban residents, the presence of religious organizations was associated with better cognition levels, but a higher number of civic organizations were linked to worse levels and a steeper decline in cognition. There were no effects of neighborhood resources on cognition among rural residents.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The differential impacts of organization types and urbanicity should be considered when promoting cognitively protective neighborhood resources for older Mexican Americans.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Associations Between Neighborhood Service, Religious, and Civic Organizations and Cognitive Decline for Older Mexican Americans Residing in Urban and Rural Areas

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>While studies have linked nature exposure to better cognitive health, little is known about the specific types or amounts needed for health benefits. Many studies regarding the health benefits of nature lack racially and ethnically diverse aging populations and have small sample sizes, limiting their generalizability. This study investigated the relationship between land cover types and cognitive function in older Mexican American adults from Wave 5 (2004–2005) of the Hispanic Established Population for the Epidemiological Study of the Elderly (EPESE) while controlling for individual and area-level covariates.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The analytic sample includes 2,069 participants (>98% of Mexican origin) aged 75 and older residing in 415 census tracts. Latent profile analysis of six land cover classifications at the census tract level identified four types: Dense Developed, Gray mix, Open Space/Agricultural, and Green-mix. Cognitive function was assessed using the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE). Key covariates include individual-level factors (e.g., age, education, and gender) and area-level factors (poverty, unemployment, and home ownership). Linear mixed-effect models adjusted for covariates were used to examine associations between land cover types and cognitive function.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Compared to other land types, individuals in greener mixed areas had better cognitive function, especially among women.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Findings suggest that environments with a mix of natural and built features may enhance cognitive health in older Mexican American women. Future research should explore how specific environmental characteristics contribute to cognitive resilience in this population.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Green, Blue, Brown, Gray? The Cognitive Benefits of Natural Environments Among Older Mexican Americans

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study examined the indirect associations between sensory impairment and cognitive function through depressive symptoms using the Actor–Partner Interdependence Mediation Model (APIMeM).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We analyzed dyadic data from 2,233 older adult couples. The outcome variable was cognitive function, while the independent variables were sensory impairments. Depressive symptoms were examined as the mediator. We utilized the APIMeM to examine within-person and cross-partner indirect associations through depressive symptoms.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Significant actor–actor indirect associations were observed for males and females in all three models, together with several cross-partner indirect associations. Dual sensory and hearing findings were generally maintained in sensitivity analyses. For vision impairment, actor–actor associations remained robust, whereas two smaller cross-partner associations were attenuated in the expanded sample.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

records.abstract: <jats:p>Social isolation is a modifiable risk factor for cognitive decline in older adults, but the mediating role of digital inclusion across settings remains unclear. We integrated a Chinese cross-sectional study (DIHA, 2024), two longitudinal cohorts (CHARLS and SHARE), and two-sample Mendelian randomization (MR) using European-ancestry genome-wide data. records.abstract: <jats:p>Older adults are most affected by cancer, yet their psychosocial experiences remain undertheorized in gerontological oncology. Using Bury’s biographical disruption as a sensitizing concept, this qualitative study develops the notion of “second biographical rupture” to examine how cancer emerges as an additional existential and relational rupture within an already transformative ageing process. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 15 older adults receiving oncology care in Türkiye. Reflexive thematic analysis showed cancer reshaping identity, autonomy, daily routines, caregiving relationships, and perceptions of dignity, dependency, and social worth. Participants described a transition from “ageing” to “waiting,” marked by suspended futures, heightened mortality awareness, social isolation, and greater reliance on family caregivers, articulating experiences from a later-life position, centred on fear of dependency and a narrowed temporal horizon. Alongside loss and dependency, some reported self-redefinition and renewed self-worth. The findings reveal critical gaps in psychosocial support, care coordination, and age-responsive geriatric oncology services.</jats:p>
title: From Ageing to Waiting: Cancer as a Second Biographical Rupture in Later Life

records.abstract: <jats:p>Cognitive impairment is associated with financial burdens on individuals and their families, yet less is known about how families change consumption patterns around the onset of cognitive decline beyond out-of-pocket medical expenditures.                     Effective, internationally transferable interventions for people with advanced dementia are needed to enhance consistent, high-quality care and quality of life. The international In-Touch project includes a cluster randomised controlled trial of an intervention to improve the quality of life for people with advanced dementia within nursing homes. A structured cultural adaptation process is crucial to ensure the In-Touch intervention retains core principles while improving local feasibility and acceptability, thereby enabling a clear assessment of fidelity. Here, we detail the cultural adaptation of the ‘In-Touch Practical Guide for Nursing Home Staff’ to enhance its feasibility, usability, and relevance across nursing homes in seven European countries. A structured cultural adaptation process, inspired by the ADAPT framework, was guided by an international team of experts, including individuals with lived experience, and dementia and palliative care researchers. Within-country group interviews were conducted in the Czech Republic, Ireland, Italy, Poland, Portugal, the Netherlands and the UK with three key participant groups: (1) nursing home staff familiar with intervention components, (2) nursing home staff unfamiliar with the intervention, and (3) family carers of people with advanced dementia. Participants (
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">n</jats:italic>
                    = 97) evaluated the guide’s clarity, cultural appropriateness, and feasibility. Cross-country consensus is presented here, with key themes including the need to simplify the guide to improve usability, ensure accessible language for all staff levels, and introduce discussion of flexibility in session length, structure, and available spaces to align with nursing home routines. Clearer guidance was needed on the roles of volunteers and family members. The guide was refined into a single, adaptable version, optimising its cultural relevance, usability, and practicality across diverse European settings. This collaborative adaptation process led to a culturally sensitive guide optimised for use in the In-Touch trial across Europe. The outlined methods can help adapt other interventions for future international palliative care research.

records.abstract: <jats:p>There is growing recognition that high-quality dementia education must be shaped by the expertise of those with lived experience. While people with dementia are increasingly involved in the development and delivery of dementia education, decisions about curriculum structure and priorities often remain led by academics with learned rather than lived experience. This paper addresses that gap by placing people with dementia at the centre of curriculum creation. In partnership with educators, people with dementia shared their insights into what health and social care professionals need to know, understand, and enact in practice to provide effective care. Nineteen online workshops were conducted with 22 people living with dementia in the United Kingdom, and two academics over an 18-month period (between January 2022 and September 2023). Three priority areas were identified, refined and validated through an iterative consensus process and thematic analysis: (1) Challenging stigma, stereotypes, and discrimination; (2) Seeing the individual and providing person-centred care; and (3) Enhancing language and communication. These priorities became the foundation of a new postgraduate module co-created through lived and learned experience. To examine how the priorities identified by people with dementia align with existing national expectations for dementia education, the themes were mapped against the Dementia Training Standards Framework (DTSF). There was strong alignment with key framework domains, particularly equality and inclusion, person-centred care, and communication, while also highlighting meaningful gaps. The co-created priorities emphasised critical reflection on professional assumptions, intersectional stigma and rights-based practice across all levels of training. The findings demonstrate how people living with dementia can play a central role in shaping dementia education, identifying priorities that both align with and extend existing curriculum standards. They highlight the value of merging lived and learned experience to ensure dementia education reflects what matters most to those living with the condition.</jats:p>
title: Co-Creating Dementia Education: What People Living With Dementia Want Health and Social Care Professionals to Know

records.abstract: <jats:p>Previous reviews have established that hearing and vision impairments are common among people living with cognitive impairment and that these comorbidities can exacerbate effects of cognitive impairments on cognitive, social and functional outcomes. This scoping review aimed to extend on this knowledge, by identifying and evaluating evidence regarding the effect of hearing and vision impairment on quality of life among older adults living with cognitive impairment, to: (i) determine if a compounding effect exists between hearing and/or vision and cognitive impairments; (ii) compare the effects on hearing, vision and health-related quality of life, and (iii) evaluate quality of life outcomes for hearing and vision interventions for this population. Seven electronic databases were searched systematically from inception to February 2026 for studies reporting quality of life outcomes among older adults living with cognitive impairment and hearing and/or vision impairment. Results were summarised then categorised by aim. Thirteen studies met inclusion criteria. The limited evidence suggests that (i) individuals living with comorbid vision and cognitive impairments may have substantially worse quality of life than those with either impairment alone, (ii) the effect is similar in size across different quality of life outcomes and (iii) sensory support interventions, involving counselling and assistance with device use, appear to be a more promising method of improving quality of life among this population. Further research is necessary to understand the relationship between hearing and vision impairments and quality of life among people living with cognitive impairment. Recommendations for future research include focusing on dual sensory impairment, utilising mixed methods approaches and inclusive selection criteria for people living with dementia. Further development and implementation of sensory support programs, codesigned with individuals with lived experience, is also recommended for improving the quality of life for people living with dementia globally.</jats:p>
title: Impact of Hearing and Vision Loss on Quality of Life in Older Adults Living With Cognitive Impairment: A Scoping Review

records.abstract: <jats:p>This narrative study explored how Chinese filial piety influences benefit finding among adult child caregivers of parents with dementia in Shanghai. Through in-depth interviews with 15 adult child caregivers of parents predominantly living with moderate dementia, we identified filial piety’s dual role: It strengthened caregivers’ role identity and moral responsibility, inspiring intrinsic motivation that enhanced benefit finding while reshaping intergenerational authority. This transformation guided caregivers to balance familial obligations with personal development in medical, daily care, and institutional care decisions, reinterpreting filial ethics through informed caregiving and emotional connection. By balancing parental well-being, filial responsibility, and caregiver sustainability, participants reconstructed filial piety through meaningful companionship, intergenerational responsibility, and self-care. This reflected an evolution from compliant filial piety to balanced filial piety. These findings highlight how culture shapes benefit finding, with implications for dementia family support that honors ethical traditions while meeting contemporary needs.</jats:p>
title: How Filial Piety Shapes Benefit Finding Among Family Caregivers: A Narrative Study Based on Adult Child Caregivers of Older Parents With Dementia

records.abstract: <jats:p>Dementia care coordinator (DCC) programmes are designed to support individuals living with dementia and their unpaid carers to navigate the complex health and social care system, ensuring access to services and information. However, the increasing number of diverse and varied programmes has resulted in a fragmented evidence base, making it challenging for policymakers, commissioners and health services researchers to fully understand and evaluate these initiatives. To address this challenge, this paper presents findings from a rapid review of reviews, designed to explore the current landscape of DCC programmes in primary and community care settings. Using a rapid approach to reviewing literature, this study includes ten evidence syntheses (including systematic, narrative, and scoping reviews) published since 2012. All included evidence syntheses focus on DCC programmes embedded in primary care or a community setting. Critical appraisals were conducted across each of the ten reviews. Findings identified a variety of terms used for DCC programmes, making it difficult to understand whether there is a difference between DCC and case manager roles. Several workforce considerations are highlighted, including the need for appropriate training, knowledge and caseload. There is also evidence to suggest that DCC programmes may improve some clinical outcomes and carer outcomes. Yet this is harder to demonstrate because programmes and their components varied considerably. This review provides decision-makers and stakeholders with a synthesis of an evolving and heterogeneous evidence base, highlighting the characteristics that appear most important for implementation and effectiveness for DCC programmes. However, the review highlights the need for consolidation of terminology, outcome measures and learning from workforce considerations to ensure sustainability of these programmes moving forward.</jats:p>
title: Dementia Care Coordinator Programmes in Primary Care and Community Settings: An International Rapid Review of Reviews

records.abstract: <jats:p>People with young-onset dementia and their family carers have unique needs, as a dementia diagnosis at a younger age profoundly impacts work, family life, and social roles. Understanding these needs is essential to develop tailored psychosocial support. This study aimed at creating a conceptual framework of needs related to young-onset dementia by exploring and prioritizing needs across different phases: before diagnosis, shortly after diagnosis, and long term. Focus groups were conducted with persons living with young-onset dementia and their family carers. Inductive qualitative analysis informed a conceptual framework, while descriptive, aggregated scores of ‘prioritization cards’ identified the urgency of needs. Before diagnosis, the most urgent need for the persons themselves and family carers was clarity, particularly regarding the diagnostic process and access to a clear care pathway. Shortly after diagnosis, key needs included coping with the diagnosis, navigating post-diagnostic support, and planning for the future, with family carers prioritizing a timely and tailored point of contact and persons living with young-onset dementia seeking clarity about disease progression. In the long term, needs focused on balancing care and autonomy within the dyad, sustaining life at home, managing transitions to residential care, and finding a meaningful way to spend the day. Family carers emphasized administrative support and persons themselves mostly valued positivity. The needs and priorities of persons living with young-onset dementia and their family carers evolve across the disease trajectory, with shifting and interdependent needs. Differences in perspectives highlight the necessity of dyadic and family-centered approaches. These insights can guide the development of tailored psychosocial interventions that address timely, phase-specific needs and support both the person living with young-onset dementia and their family.</jats:p>
title: Understanding and Prioritizing Needs of People With Young-Onset Dementia and Family Carers Across the Disease Trajectory: A Qualitative Study and Conceptual Framework

                    <jats:title>BACKGROUND</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The impact of cerebral amyloid pathology on cognitive and functional decline may differ with age. Evidence linking brain amyloidopathy to physical decline remains limited and inconsistent. This study investigated the association between brain amyloid status and cognitive and physical decline in (pre)frail older adults with cognitive impairment.</jats:p>

                    <jats:title>METHODS</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This longitudinal analysis used data from the CogFrail study. Brain amyloid pathology was assessed using amyloid-positron emission tomography (visual reading). Linear mixed-effects models examined differences over a two-year follow-up between amyloid-positive and amyloid-negative participants in cognitive, functional, and physical trajectories. Cognitive and functional outcomes included the Mini-Mental State Examination, the Clinical Dementia Rating–Sum of Boxes, the Activities of Daily Living Index, and a neuropsychological battery, while the physical domain was assessed using handgrip strength, chair rise time, gait speed, and the Short Physical Performance Battery.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>RESULTS</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Among 199 participants (mean age 82.3 ± 4.8 years; 65.3% women), 108(54.3%) were amyloid-positive. Amyloid-positive participants experienced greater decline in the Clinical Dementia Rating–Sum of Boxes (β = 0.30, 95% CI 0.10–0.49; p = 0.003, log-transformed) and the Mini-Mental State Examination (β = –1.62, 95% CI –2.74 to –0.49; p = 0.005). No significant longitudinal differences were observed between groups in the Activities of Daily Living Index, neuropsychological outcomes, or physical performance measures.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>CONCLUSION</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Amyloid pathology assessment may help differentiate cognitive trajectories in cognitively impaired (pre)frail older adults. Greater cognitive decline in amyloid-positive participants was not associated with greater loss of independence or additional physical decline over time.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>TRIAL REGISTRATION</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>NCT03129269</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Association between Brain Amyloid Status and Cognitive and Physical Performance in Older Adults with Frailty Criteria: Longitudinal Data from the CogFrail Study

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Prolonged heterochronic parabiosis (HPB) reduces DNA methylation (DNAm) age in old mice, but how age-opposing methylation changes are organized across tissues and retained after removal of youthful circulation is unclear. We analyzed processed reduced-representation bisulfite sequencing data from 78 blood and liver samples from a published prolonged-HPB experiment. Across 1,008,133 CpGs with at least 10-fold coverage in every sample, we quantified normal-aging and HPB effects, defined directional reversal by effect size, tested exact cross-tissue and post-detachment persistence, and used chromosome-aware null models for overlap and gene-convergence analyses. HPB-associated methylation changes opposed normal aging in blood and liver, including in independent-cohort comparisons that avoided a shared Old-ISO reference. At the primary 10-percentage-point threshold, 22,424 blood and 22,286 liver CpGs were reversed immediately after HPB; 1,792 were shared at identical loci. After two months of recovery, 25,867 blood and 15,437 liver CpGs were reversed, with 1,387 exact shared loci. A 64-CpG cross-tissue core persisted across both time points. Reversed CpGs were depleted from promoters and CpG islands and enriched in gene bodies and open-sea regions. After exact shared CpGs were removed, tissue-specific sites showed a modest excess of nearest-gene convergence (4,716 observed vs 4,215 expected; empirical P≈.001), whereas promoter/gene-body and Gene Ontology convergence were not supported by stricter genomic null models. Youthful circulation produces both conserved and tissue-specific reversal of age-associated methylation. Persistence after detachment and modest cross-tissue genomic-neighborhood convergence suggest that systemic rejuvenation is encoded at multiple levels of epigenomic organization.</jats:p>
title: Youthful circulation reshapes age-associated DNA methylation across blood and liver

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Chronodisruption is increasingly recognised as a fundamental driver of biological aging rather than merely a consequence of advancing age. Although substantial evidence links circadian dysfunction with individual age-related diseases, the mechanistic integration of chronodisruption across the hallmarks of aging and its therapeutic implications remains fragmented. This review provides a comprehensive synthesis of current evidence describing how age-associated deterioration of the circadian timing system interacts with established hallmarks of aging, including genomic instability, epigenetic alterations, mitochondrial dysfunction, dysregulated nutrient sensing, impaired proteostasis, chronic inflammation, and cellular senescence. This article also incorporates how these interconnected mechanisms contribute to the development and progression of major age-related disorders, including neurodegenerative, cardiovascular, metabolic diseases, and cancer, highlighting shared molecular regulators such as BMAL1, CLOCK, PER, CRY, REV-ERBs, SIRT1, AMPK, and mTOR. Although several reviews exist that focus on individual diseases or isolated circadian mechanisms, this review integrates molecular, cellular, and translational evidence into a unified framework linking chronodisruption to systemic aging. This article discusses emerging chronotherapeutic strategies including chrono-phototherapy, chrono-nutrition, chrono-exercise, natural chrono-modulators, chrono-pharmacology, and precision geromedicine that aim to restore circadian homeostasis and improve healthy aging. Collectively, this review identifies circadian rhythm restoration as a promising systems-level therapeutic approach and outlines future directions for integrating chronobiology into precision interventions for age-related diseases.</jats:p>
title: Chronobiology of Aging: Interactions Between Circadian Rhythms, Oxidative Stress, and Inflammation

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In adults and older adults, pain is inversely associated with self-rated health (SRH) independent of health status. Less is known about this association in the very old. This paper aims to determine how pain is associated with SRH in very old people with and without adjustment for individual health status.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using data from five cohorts of very old people aged 80+ from different cultural contexts (n=2,664), we separately fitted single- and multi-level logistic models of SRH to examine cross-sectional and longitudinal associations with pain, respectively. We performed random effects meta-analysis to combine cohort-specific odds ratios (ORs) of positive SRH (selecting response options ‘good’ and above) for those reporting any pain in the past month, at baseline and then over time for up to 10 years follow-up, with adjustment for sociodemographic (age, sex, income status) and individual health (multimorbidity, depressive symptoms, functional ability) variables.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Over half of participants across cohorts (55.4%) reported having pain and 71.1% had positive SRH at baseline. At baseline, the odds of positive SRH were significantly lower in those with pain in all cohorts when we adjusted for sociodemographic variables (combined OR 0.37; 95% CI 0.28, 0.48), which persisted when we added health-related variables to the models (combined OR 0.42; 95% CI 0.34, 0.54). In longitudinal analysis, over time pain remained significantly associated with lower odds of positive SRH throughout follow-up (combined OR 0.45; 95% CI 0.35, 0.58) after adjusting for sociodemographic and individual health variables.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Pain is common in very old people, and it is associated with worse SRH independent of health status at baseline and over time. This inverse association is consistent across cultures and time, highlighting the importance of addressing pain in this age group.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Pain and self-rated health in the very old: Individual participant data meta-analysis from five TULIP Consortium cohorts

records.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Patients with multimorbidity face multiple care demands, including the time to access care and the cognitive effort of coordinating care. It is unclear how patients’ experiences with care continuity, coordination, and time burdens (i.e., health care contact days) vary across multimorbidity groups or what role potential protective factors may play.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This cross-sectional study used the nationally representative 2022 Medicare Current Beneficiary Survey linked with traditional Medicare claims from the United States. We included continuously enrolled, community-dwelling adults aged ≥ 65 with ≥ 2 chronic conditions. We described self-reported experiences of care continuity and care coordination, health care contact days (receiving ambulatory or institutional care), and telehealth days, home visits, and remote monitoring by multimorbidity group (low: 2–3 chronic conditions, medium: 4–6, high: 7+).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Among 4424 respondents, care experiences varied by multimorbidity group. Adults in the high multimorbidity group often reported having a usual source of care (96.6%), one provider knowing all of their medical needs (84.4%), and their primary care physician (PCP) being informed about specialist care (81.3%). Fewer patients in the medium and high multimorbidity groups reported satisfaction with co-localized care and ease of managing care, while fewer patients in the low multimorbidity group reported satisfaction with specialist availability. Mean contact days ranged from 12.6 (SD 13.4) per year (low multimorbidity group) to 31.3 (SD 23.9) (high multimorbidity). More patients in the high multimorbidity group used telehealth, home care, and remote monitoring.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Care experiences vary across multimorbidity groups, with high-multimorbidity patients experiencing greater continuity but also greater difficulty managing care. The findings suggest a potential need to improve specialist access and informational continuity in the low multimorbidity group, support care management and co-localized care in the higher multimorbidity groups and reduce care complexity and potentially avoidable contact days across multimorbidity groups.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Differential care demands on Medicare patients by multimorbidity group: care continuity, care coordination, and contact days

records.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The Age-Friendly Cities and Communities Questionnaire (AFCCQ) measures how older people perceive the age-friendliness of their city or community. With 23% of Swedish residents projected to be aged ≥ 65 years by 2040, a culturally adapted and psychometrically validated Swedish version (AFCCQ-SE) is needed to guide age-friendly initiatives nationally. This study aimed to translate the AFCCQ into Swedish and to conduct its cross-cultural adaptation and psychometric validation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In Phase I, the AFCCQ-EN was independently forward-translated into Swedish and back-translated into English. Ten older adults and ten academic experts then rated each item’s relevance on a 4-point scale. In Phase II, 874 community-dwelling Swedes aged ≥ 65 years (64.9% female; mean age 75.7 ± 5.8 years; 82.8% urban) from two regions completed the AFCCQ-SE. Confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) was used to assess the nine-domain structure against fit criteria and composite reliability (CR) was used to evaluate internal consistency. Rasch analysis examined various aspects of the AFCCQ at the item and rating scale level.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      I-CVI values of all items ranged from 0.80 to 1.00 (mostly 0.90). CFA supported the proposed nine-domain structure (χ²[194] = 562.9; normed χ² = 2.90; CFI = 0.962; TLI = 0.951; SRMR = 0.0335; RMSEA = 0.047). CR values were acceptable across most domains (0.783–0.937), with two domains marginally below the threshold (0.658–0.699). Rasch analyses showed acceptable rating categories and satisfactory item fit. Urban–rural DIF was found for two transportation items (0.51 & 0.71 logits, Holm adjusted
                      <jats:italic>p =</jats:italic>
                       0.000). PCA supported unidimensionality within each domain rather than for the questionnaire as a whole. Twenty-two item pairs showed local dependence (
                      <jats:italic>r</jats:italic>
                       = 0.16–0.84), 21 of them within a single domain. Aggregating the items into nine testlets largely resolved local dependence (largest residual correlation = 0.10), and the first residual contrast eigenvalue decreased from 3.32 to 1.52 (< 2.0), supporting unidimensionality of the testlet model.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This AFCCQ-SE study, using both CFA and Rasch analysis, provided preliminary support for its psychometric properties in this Swedish sample. Further validation using samples from larger regions and longitudinal study designs is needed to verify these findings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Translation, cultural adaptation and psychometric evaluation of the age-friendly cities and communities questionnaire for Sweden

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Muscle strength and muscle quantity may become dissociated with aging, but whether strength relative to directly measured appendicular lean mass is associated with life functioning remains uncertain. We examined whether handgrip strength relative to dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA)-measured appendicular lean mass was associated with life functioning in older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This cross-sectional study used nationally representative data from the 2024 Korea National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey. Participants were 1,133 adults aged 65 years or older with valid DXA-derived appendicular lean mass, maximal handgrip strength, and 10-item Life Functioning Scale (LF-10) data. Within each sex, maximal handgrip strength was regressed on appendicular lean mass using survey weights, and the standardized observed-minus-predicted residual represented relative strength. Survey-weighted regression accounted for sampling weights, strata, and clusters. Secondary, supplementary, and exploratory analyses examined EQ-5D-3L ​utility, phase angle, and falls, respectively.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      The fully adjusted analysis included 1,069 participants. Each 1-standard-deviation higher relative strength was associated with a 2.95-point higher LF-10 score (95% confidence interval [CI], 2.08–3.82;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                       < 0.001). Compared with the lowest quartile, the highest quartile had a 7.80-point higher LF-10 score (95% CI, 5.62–9.98;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                       < 0.001). Model-adjusted mean LF-10 scores increased from 85.30 (95% CI, 83.21–87.38) in the lowest quartile to 93.09 (95% CI, 91.87–94.32) in the highest. The association was approximately linear (P for nonlinearity = 0.202) and remained similar across sensitivity analyses. Higher relative strength was also associated with higher EQ-5D utility and phase angle, whereas the association with falls was not statistically significant.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In older Korean adults, handgrip strength relative to DXA-measured appendicular lean mass was associated with better life functioning. This population-referenced measure may help characterize functional heterogeneity not apparent from muscle quantity alone but does not establish a diagnostic or clinically actionable index. Prospective and external validation are needed before clinical application.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Handgrip strength relative to DXA-measured appendicular lean mass and life functioning in older Korean adults: a nationwide cross-sectional study

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Functional reserve is difficult to characterize during routine acute hospital care. Sarcopenia is associated with frailty, disability, and mortality, but rapid functional assessment remains underused in hospitalized older adults. We evaluated handgrip strength and 4-meter walk test (4MWT) performance as pragmatic measures of probable sarcopenia and physiologic reserve during acute illness.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We conducted a prospective cohort study of 279 hospitalized adults aged 65–95 years at a tertiary medical center. Handgrip strength was measured using dynamometry; values < 27 kg in men and < 16 kg in women were classified as probable sarcopenia according to EWGSOP2. Among 169 participants who completed the 4MWT without an assistive device, associations between probable sarcopenia, walk time, age, and sex were evaluated using linear regression. Selection into the 4MWT subgroup was examined using inverse-probability weighting (IPW).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Participants with probable sarcopenia were underrepresented in the 4MWT subgroup. In the 169 participants with eligible 4MWT measurements, probable sarcopenia was independently associated with a 1.59-second longer walk time after adjustment for age and sex (95% CI 0.55–2.63;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                       = 0.003). The IPW estimate was similar (β = 1.62 s, 95% CI 0.49–2.75;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                       = 0.005). In an exploratory overlapping age-window analysis, concordance was greatest in the 73–84-year interval (AUC = 0.69, bootstrap 95% CI 0.58–0.80).
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Handgrip strength is a rapid bedside-feasible measure, whereas the 4MWT is a complementary ward-based assessment for sufficiently mobile and clinically stable hospitalized older adults. These state-dependent measures characterize functional performance and physiologic reserve during acute illness; longitudinal studies are required to determine their relationship to baseline function, recovery, and healthspan outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Handgrip strength and 4-meter walk performance as practical functional measures of sarcopenia and physiologic reserve in acute hospital care: a prospective cohort study

records.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Sarcopenia is common in older adults and predicts adverse outcomes. Contemporary consensus definitions use low muscle strength as the entry point for case-finding, but confirmation requires demonstration of low muscle mass, typically quantified by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) or bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA), which are not universally accessible. Quadriceps strength is functionally central to lower-limb health and can be objectively measured by concentric dynamometry. However, previous concentric studies in sarcopenia have typically assessed a single, usually dominant, limb, and the relative contribution of the dominant and non-dominant limbs to the association with muscle mass has not been examined. We therefore compared concentric knee muscle performance between the dominant and non-dominant limbs and examined the association of dominant and non-dominant limb quadriceps strength with low skeletal muscle mass index (low SMI) in community-dwelling older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In this cross-sectional study, community-dwelling adults aged ≥ 60 years underwent concentric knee strength testing at an angular velocity of 60°/s. Peak torque, total work, and average power of the quadriceps and hamstrings were measured bilaterally, and the hamstring-to-quadriceps (H: Q) ratio was calculated. Leg dominance was self-reported, and right- and left-side values were reassigned to the dominant and non-dominant limbs. Participants were classified as normal SMI or low SMI using sex-specific Asian Working Group for Sarcopenia (AWGS) 2019 criteria. Paired t-tests compared dominant and non-dominant limb variables; age- and sex-adjusted binary logistic regression, receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis with DeLong comparison, and a mixed-design (limb SMI group) analysis evaluated the contribution of each limb to low SMI.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      A total of 171 participants were included in the analysis (139 normal SMI, 32 low SMI; mean age 69.88 ± 7.97 years). Dominant limb quadriceps peak torque, total work, and average power were significantly greater than the corresponding non-dominant limb values (all
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       ≤ 0.004), whereas hamstring variables showed no significant between-limb differences. In adjusted models, higher quadriceps peak torque, total work, and average power of the dominant limb were associated with lower odds of low SMI (odds ratios [ORs] 0.968, 0.993, and 0.958; all
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       ≤ 0.010); in the non-dominant limb, total work and average power were significantly associated (ORs 0.994 and 0.966;
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.049 and 0.030), whereas peak torque was not (OR 0.976;
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.058). The limb × SMI group interaction was not significant for any quadriceps variable (all
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       > 0.10). Area-under-the-curve (AUC) values were similar for the dominant (0.63–0.64) and non-dominant limbs (0.60–0.64; all DeLong
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       ≥ 0.34), and all remained below 0.70.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Lower quadriceps strength in both the dominant and non-dominant limbs was associated with low SMI, and neither limb contributed disproportionately to this association or showed superior discriminative ability. These findings indicate a bilateral reduction in knee-extensor strength that is independent of limb dominance; given the modest discrimination, quadriceps concentric strength should complement, rather than replace, established muscle mass assessment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Association between dominant and non-dominant limb concentric quadriceps strength and low skeletal muscle mass index in community-dwelling older adults: a cross-sectional study

records.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Long-term care policy and practice continue to promote institutional living at the expense of support for ageing in place. Improving experiences of care home residents requires recognising care homes as places of everyday living, moving beyond clinical models to support ‘living with care’ rather than ‘existing in care’. Staff uniforms are ubiquitous in care homes yet remain relatively unexamined. Unlike hospitals, care homes are places where older people live, and uniforms may contribute to the medicalisation of ageing. Non-uniform approaches could support home-like environments and resident wellbeing. An emerging trend of non-uniform dress codes in UK care homes warrants evidence synthesis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We conducted a scoping review in accordance with PRISMA-ScR guidelines, searching six bibliographic databases to April 2026. Supplementary searches of care sector websites, charity platforms, and public discussion forums captured perspectives beyond academic literature. Included sources spanned empirical studies and non-academic public content addressing staff clothing in care homes for older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Fifty-eight records were included, describing 13 empirical studies and 36 public discourse cases; only a minority of research records (8; 35%) were peer-reviewed. Seven themes were identified: health and hygiene; identification, care home atmosphere; changing behaviours; perspectives and preferences; perceptions and connotations; and decision making. Despite a limited evidence base, available research suggests non-uniform policies do not compromise hygiene or resident health, and may reduce anxiety, support independence and foster relational, homelike environments. Public discourse presented a more contested picture, with both approaches carrying perceived advantages and tensions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Staff clothing is a socially embedded aspect of care practice. Research evidence suggests non-uniform policies do not compromise safety and may actively support resident wellbeing and relational engagement. However, public discourse reflects genuine concerns around professionalism, identification and individuality that empirical research has not fully addressed. Context-sensitive, resident-centred decision making and research prioritising direct engagement with residents are needed.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Staff clothing and uniforms in care homes for older people: a scoping review and analysis of online content

records.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Extreme heat is an increasing threat to the health and wellbeing of older adults, particularly those living in densely populated urban environments with poor housing conditions and limited access to cooling resources. Community-based heat-health interventions have been proposed as an important climate adaptation strategy to reduce heat-related vulnerability among older adults, yet little is known about how such interventions are implemented in real-world settings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      This qualitative case study examined how two nongovernmental organizations (NGOs) implemented a community-based heat-health intervention for vulnerable older adults in Hong Kong. Data were drawn from observations of 51 home visits and 7 community activities, case conference notes, and four semi-structured focus groups with frontline and management staff (
                      <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                       = 18). Inductive thematic analysis was used to explore how organizational approaches, local contexts, and service-delivery models shaped implementation.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Although both NGOs implemented the same core intervention components, they adopted different service-delivery models. NGO 1 employed a relationship-centered approach emphasizing continuity of care, individualized assessment, and trust-building. This approach facilitated rapport-building, individualized support, and identification of misconceptions and environmental risks, but required substantial staff time and resources to maintain continuity of care and individualized engagement. NGO 2 adopted a standardized, outreach-oriented model designed to maximize community outreach, visibility, and awareness. This approach increased visibility and facilitated broad distribution of cooling resources but was sometimes constrained by the diverse housing conditions and complex needs of older adults. Housing characteristics, social isolation, and environmental constraints influenced how both approaches were implemented in practice. Collaboration with an academic team supported ongoing adaptation and capacity building throughout implementation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Community-based heat-health interventions can play an important role in protecting older adults from heat-related health risks and supporting climate adaptation in ageing populations, but different delivery models involve distinct implementation strengths and challenges. Relationship-centered approaches may be particularly valuable when ongoing assessment, trust-building, and individualized support are required, whereas outreach-oriented approaches may promote awareness of heat-health risks and community engagement. The findings highlight the importance of aligning intervention strategies with the needs and living environments of older adults and suggest that community-based adaptation efforts should be accompanied by broader policies addressing housing-related heat vulnerability.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Clinical trial number</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>not applicable.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Implementing community-based heat-health interventions for older adults: a comparative case study of two NGO delivery models in Hong Kong
