<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Social isolation is an urgent public health concern, especially for older immigrants who face heightened barriers to social participation due to disability, structural health inequities, and limited access to culturally and linguistically appropriate services. This study presents a programmatic model that explains how social connection and sustained participation can be fostered through accessible, culturally responsive, and participatory design.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This community-engaged case study examines a national virtual program serving Spanish-speaking older adults, many of whom have sensory disabilities and chronic illnesses. A thematic and comparative analysis was conducted using qualitative interviews with ten older adults with vision impairment, program documents, and consultation with program leadership. This led to the identification of a programmatic model, the emergent connections platform.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The emergent connections platform strengthens loosely connected social networks among older adults who share cultural and lived experiences through three pillars. The first is cultural, linguistic, and physically accessible infrastructure. Second, shared governance cultivates member leadership and program co-creation. Third, a flexible structure allows for evolution in response to member needs and innovations. These pillars collectively create pathways for individuals to engage, lead, and strengthen their communities.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Advancing a more inclusive democracy requires sustained investment in accessible, community-led initiatives that support the leadership and innovation of marginalized older adults. This calls for moving towards models that position older adults as co-creators of programs and services. Doing so cultivates social connection through leadership, reciprocity, and a sense of belonging within a broader social fabric.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Emergent Connections: A Community-Based Model for Advancing Social Connection Among Immigrant Older Adults with Disabilities

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The global aging population has led to an increasing number of older active drivers. While age-related physical and cognitive changes are associated with increased crash risk, specific on-road adaptations and safety outcomes of older drivers remain unclear. This study examined distinct driving characteristics, personality traits, and cognitive processes related to decision-making among middle-aged and older drivers in a simulated driving environment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We assessed driving performance in a high-fidelity motorcycle simulator across drivers in three age groups: middle-aged (30-54; n = 40), aged 65–74 (n = 34), and aged 75 + (75-86; n = 29). Comparative analysis focused on speed regulation, braking behavior, control stability, and accident rates. Additionally, questionnaire measures and a computerized decision-making task were employed to assess risk perception and risky decision-making.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Compared to the middle-aged group, both older groups demonstrated a significantly more conservative driving profile: lower mean speeds, fewer speeding violations, longer braking maneuvers, reduced variation in throttle control, and a lower incidence of simulated accidents. Drivers aged 75+ also reported higher perceived risk in driving scenarios and displayed diminished discrimination between risk and non-risk situations in a braking decision task. Mediation analyses showed that steering variance in the simulator and self-reported health/safety risk-taking significantly mediated the relationship between age group and number of accidents.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings indicate that older drivers adopt proactive compensatory strategies that could result in fewer simulated accidents. These findings challenge a purely deficit-oriented perspective on older driver safety, underscoring the critical role of behavioral adaptation and strategic self-regulation in maintaining safe mobility.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Adaptive driving, not unsafe: Older drivers’ compensatory strategies and lower simulated crash risk

records.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The extant literature suggests that spending time helping others is associated with both beneficial and detrimental effects on givers’ emotional experiences. To reconcile these findings, the current study examined the daily- and monthly-level associations between spending time helping others and well-being. We predicted that spending time helping others would be associated with lower hedonic well-being at the daily level but higher eudaimonic well-being at the monthly level. We further hypothesized that age would moderate these associations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We used data from the main survey and the National Study of Daily Experiences (NSDE) in MIDUS 3 (N=865) and MIDUS Refresher 1 (N=612). Participants reported their daily and monthly time spent helping others. Measures included hedonic well-being (negative affect and positive affect) and eudaimonic well-being (social and psychological well-being).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>At the daily level, our sample of adults experienced mixed emotional consequences on days when they spent more time helping others, reporting both higher negative and positive affect. Age moderation showed young and middle-aged adults experienced more negative affect. At the monthly level, spending time helping others was associated with higher social and psychological well-being. This association was significantly stronger among older adults than middle-aged adults in Refresher 1. Monthly spending time helping others was not associated with hedonic well-being.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings suggest that spending time helping others can be both taxing and enjoyable in the short term while contributing to eudaimonic benefits over the long term. Older age may reduce costs and enhance benefits of spending time helping others.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Spending time helping others and well-being of givers: Age differences in immediate and long-term effects on well-being

records.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Prior research finds that women spend more years than men caring for older relatives and friends (“lifetime family caregiving”) in the United States. This study examines whether these amounts have changed in recent years (2023 vs. 2011) and how recent estimates differ for men and women by relationship to the care recipient and type of care provided.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We update and expand previously published estimates, drawing upon the National Study of Caregiving (n=1,972 in 2011; n=6,500 in 2021-2023) and the Current Population Survey. We use a demographic technique to calculate years of remaining life men and women ages 20+ would provide family caregiving to an older adult if current age-specific rates held.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In 2023, lifetime family caregiving for an older adult was nearly three years longer for women relative to men: 7.1 (95%CI: 6.2,8.0) vs. 4.2 (95%CI: 3.7,4.7) (p&lt;.001). For women, estimates for lifetime family caregiving were a year higher in 2023 than in 2011 (p=.03); for men, estimates were nearly identical in both years. In 2023, lifetime family caregiving for an older spouse or partner was similar for women and men but was higher for women than for men for caring for a parent, grandparent, and other relationship and for personal, household, transportation, and medical tasks.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Our results indicate lifetime family caregiving has increased for women. Gaps in lifetime family caregiving for men and women may grow further as late-life care needs increase and the percentage of older adults without close kin continues to rise.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Lifetime family caregiving for older U.S. adults by men and women, 2011 and 2023

records.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Early population-based screening for Alzheimer’s disease remains limited by the scalability and accessibility of conventional biomarker testing. We tested whether passive naturalistic driving changes predict progression from cognitively normal status to sustained mild cognitive impairment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Season-adjusted monthly driving data from 298 older adults, including 25 progressors, were summarized into within-person trajectory features capturing drift and instability in cornering and destination diversity relative to a six-month baseline. A GEE logistic regression was evaluated under leave-one-out cross-validation with a paired-consecutive flagging rule. Landmark survival analyses at 12 and 24 months assessed prognostic value. Five held-out clinical subgroups (n = 82 evaluable), plasma pTau217, MoCA trajectories, and depression scores provided independent post hoc validation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The model detected 19/25 progressors (AUC=0.752, 95%CI: 0.627–0.863; 76% sensitivity; 75% specificity) with an 18-month median lead time before sustained CDR conversion. Adding static baseline driving features reduced discrimination (AUC=0.702), supporting that within-person driving change, not absolute level, carries a predictive signal. Driving markers stratified risk at 12 months (HR = 6.02, 95%CI: 2.35–15.41) and 24 months (HR = 13.38, 95%CI: 3.03–59.04). Signals converged or were directionally consistent with higher pTau217 among detected progressors and clinically ambiguous single-endpoint cases, whereas flagged stable participants showed MoCA decline without pTau217 enrichment. Depressive symptoms did not explain the driving signal (Spearman rho=0.05, p=0.53). The sustained conversion rate (12.3/1,000 person-years) matched epidemiological expectations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Scalable driving-trajectory features can detect preclinical functional decline with clinically meaningful lead time, without demographic, genetic, or cognitive data, and may serve as an objective neurobehavioral screening tool.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Naturalistic Driving Engineered Trajectories Forecast Future Cognitive Decline

records.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Family caregivers of individuals with Alzheimer’s Disease and Related Dementias (ADRD) work with healthcare providers to ensure effective care coordination on behalf of the care recipient. However, challenges within the caregiver-healthcare provider relationship are common and may contribute to poor caregiver health outcomes. This study examined the impact of the perceived quality of the relationship between family caregivers and healthcare providers and the caregivers’ daily mental health symptom burden (depressive symptoms, anxiety, and stress).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study included 228 family caregivers who lived with and provided unpaid care to a family member with dementia. Linear Mixed-Effects Models (LMM) were developed to assess whether the caregiver-provider relationship was associated with caregiver daily depressive symptoms, daily anxiety, and daily stress.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Of 228 caregivers, 82% were female, 84% were spouses or partners of the care recipient, and 9% of caregivers were classified as living in poverty. Caregivers who rated their providers’ affect (perceptions of being valued, respected, and emotionally supported) more positively reported lower daily depressive symptoms (β = −0.06, p = .001) and anxiety symptoms (β = −0.07, p &lt; .001). The caregiver-provider relationship was not associated with daily stress experiences.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Findings from the study suggest that healthcare provider affect (perceptions of being valued, respected, and emotionally supported) may be a protective factor, especially against depressive symptoms and anxiety, and offer an avenue for future interventions. Integrating caregiver-provider relationship-informed practices into routine dementia care may help foster emotionally responsive, person- and family-centered care.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Caregiver-provider relationship quality and health outcomes in family caregivers of people living with dementia

                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study examines the association between reduced social engagement and cognitive function among older adults in China during the COVID-19 pandemic with a focus on gender and urban–rural differences.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study data, we used OLS regression to assess changes in cognitive function before and during the pandemic and their associations with changes in physical and cognitively stimulating activities.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Cognitive function declined across social groups, with the largest decline among urban women. Moderate physical activity was not associated with less cognitive function, whereas decreased engagement in cognitively stimulating activities was associated with greater decline.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Forms of social engagement were associated with cognitive function of older adults in distinct ways, underscoring the need for a nuanced rather than uniform interpretation. The observed differences in cognitive function by subgroups suggest a need for targeted interventions to support older populations in the post-pandemic context.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Social Engagement and Cognitive Function Among Chinese Older Adults During the COVID-19 Outbreak: Gender and Urban–Rural Disparities

                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study examined the longitudinal effects of social isolation on chronic diseases and depressive symptoms among middle-aged and older adults in South Korea, with attention to gender and age differences.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using data from three waves of the Korean Longitudinal Study of Aging, longitudinal path analysis was conducted on 5,585 participants.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Women and older adults showed higher levels of social isolation, chronic diseases, and depressive symptoms, indicating greater vulnerability. Significant longitudinal and bidirectional associations emerged among social isolation, chronic diseases, and depressive symptoms over time. While gender differences in long-term patterns were modest, age-related disparities were more substantial.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings underscore the importance of strengthening community-based social networks and implementing both conventional outreach—such as home visits—and innovative approaches, including technology-assisted companionship, to identify socially isolated individuals, particularly older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: A Longitudinal Study on Social Isolation, Chronic Diseases, and Depressive Symptoms: Evidence From the Korean Longitudinal Study of Aging

                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study investigated whether cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF) in young adulthood is associated with depressive symptoms several decades later and if later-life physical activity and self-rated health mediate this association.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The sample comprised 690 Swedish men completing a CRF test at age 18 and self-reported depressive symptoms around age 61. Unadjusted and adjusted logistic and linear regression models and Bayesian mediation analyses were estimated.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Medium and high CRF at age 18, compared with low CRF, were associated with lower odds of clinically significant depressive symptoms in late adulthood. The odds ratios of clinically significant depressive symptoms were 0.329 (95% CI [0.157, 0.687]) for men with medium and 0.383 (95% CI [0.157, 0.939]) for men with high CRF compared with those with low CRF. No credible mediated associations were observed.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings suggest that promoting fitness early in life may represent a useful preventive strategy for mental health resilience across the life course.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Cardiorespiratory Fitness in Young Adulthood and Depressive Symptoms Later in Life Among Swedish Men

                    Relocation is an option for older adults who leave their home to improve their emotional well-being, physical health, and safety. Moves can enhance agency or foster a loss of empowerment. We explored older adults’ transition experiences from a community setting to a retirement community and created messaging to help with experiences of older adults and their self-identified family or friend caregivers. We conducted 30 telephone interviews and analyzed relocation experiences, which informed
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">I Did It My Way Theatre.</jats:italic>

Our goal was to ease the transition experiences by disseminating findings to those involved in similar relocation situations. Attendees completed a post-performance questionnaire asking how the play helped them understand relocation and held table discussions concerning production themes. Follow-up interviews with 11 participants revealed that the play delivered hard messages in an impactful way.

title: I Did It My Way Theatre: Research and Live Theatre as Applied to the Transition of Relocating Older Adults

records.abstract: <jats:p>Knowledge of dementia facilitates early detection, care planning, and stigma reduction, yet less is known about dementia knowledge among Asian American populations. This study examined correlates of dementia knowledge among 505 Chinese, Korean, and Vietnamese Americans aged 50 and older residing in Central Florida. Dementia knowledge was assessed using the Dementia Knowledge Assessment Scale with four subscales. Linear regression analyses examined associations of dementia knowledge with sociodemographic, immigration, social, digital and information, and dementia experiences and attitudinal factors. Participants demonstrated low overall dementia knowledge. Digital literacy was positively associated with total dementia knowledge and all subscales except communication and behavior. Limited English proficiency was negatively associated with knowledge in the causes and characteristics subscale. The perceived importance of dementia planning was positively associated with total dementia knowledge and three subscales. Subscale-specific findings should be interpreted cautiously because of varying subscale reliability, particularly for communication and behavior.</jats:p>
title: Dementia Knowledge Among Older Asian Americans: Roles of Digital Literacy, Planning Attitudes, and Sociocultural Contexts

                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Neighborhood satisfaction is a key indicator of well-being and community quality of life, yet its relationship with third place engagement remains underexplored.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study examines how third place engagement, access, and perceived built environments relate to physical livability, social connectedness, and overall neighborhood satisfaction among older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Survey data were collected from 515 adults aged 65 and older in the Orlando area, and separate Ordinary Least Squares regression models were used.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The results indicate that neighborhood satisfaction is multidimensional, with shared yet distinct correlates across domains. Third place engagement and walkable access were consistently associated with all three outcomes. Socially oriented third place use was more closely tied to social connectedness, while built environment quality aligned with physical livability. Overall satisfaction reflected both domains, highlighting the value of viewing neighborhood satisfaction as related but distinct constructs shaped by functional and social experiences among older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Third Places, Walkable Access, and Neighborhood Satisfaction Among Older Adults

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Older Australian adults commonly engage in formal and informal volunteering. We examine how volunteering relates to social support, a combined measure of an individual’s quantity of social interactions, and satisfaction with the quality of social relationships.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Data were analysed from 932 adults aged 50–70 years, surveyed between September 2023 and July 2024 (54.4% male).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Formal volunteering at < 5, 5–10, and 10+ hours/week was associated with higher social support (β = 0.54; β = 1.21; β = 1.61), as was providing <5 hours/week of informal childcare (β = 1.02). Social interaction increased across all levels of formal volunteering (β = 0.35; β = 1.01; β = 1.22), and providing <5 hours/week of care to children (β = 0.49). Social satisfaction showed no significant associations. Offering informal care to adults was not associated with any changes in social support.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Formal volunteering appears to enhance social interaction, but not satisfaction, which may have implications for social prescribing practices.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Social Support, Interactions, and Satisfaction Among Older Australian Adults Engaged in Formal and Informal Volunteering: A Cross-Sectional Analysis

records.abstract: <jats:p>Internalized ageist and ableist beliefs significantly influence health outcomes, happiness, and longevity. Idealization of youth and pervasive ageist and ableist narratives devalue aging, contributing to perceptions of later life and potentially fostering grief over lost opportunities. To develop evidence-based interventions, it is essential to examine the potential relationship between grief, yearning, and fears about aging. A cross-sectional survey was conducted using ResearchMatch, and 384 individuals responded to questions regarding ageism, ableism, and experiences with grief. Yearning was significantly associated with internalized ageism, excessive fear of aging, and loss of physical health. Grief was significantly associated with age, internalized ageism, and excessive fear of aging. Interventions to address feelings of loss as we age, both experienced and anticipated, can be developed to address and improve personal attitudes toward growing older.</jats:p>
title: Yearning to Be Our Younger Self: The Relationship Between Grief and Yearning to Internalized Ageism and Ableism

records.abstract: <jats:p>This study aimed to compare the differences in life-space activities among older Japanese drivers based on self-reported driving engagement in relatively difficult situations. This is a cross-sectional cohort study of 12,309 community-dwelling older drivers (mean [SD] age, 72.5 [5.1] years; 54.5% female). Driving engagement was assessed using yes/no questions regarding six driving situations, including rain, dark nights, and unfamiliar roads. Responses to the situations were categorized as “not driving,” “driving with anxiety,” and “driving without anxiety.” The Active Mobility Index (AMI) assessed the life-space and activities from respondents’ home. Analysis of covariance showed that driving with anxiety and not driving in some situations were significantly lower AMI scores compared to driving without anxiety (p < 0.05), especially in those who drive ≥ 4 situations. While driving is a correlate of life-space activities in older adults, addressing driving anxiety may help maintain life-space mobility among older drivers.</jats:p>
title: Comparison of Life-Space Activities by Driving Engagement Among Older Drivers

                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Falls are a major cause of morbidity and functional decline among older adults, yet early gait-based markers of fall risk remain unclear.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To examine age-related differences in spatiotemporal gait parameters and their associations with fall risk among older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Two hundred participants aged 65 years or older were classified into four age groups and two fall-risk levels using a standardized Fall Risk Assessment. Gait parameters were measured with the IB-GAIT system.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      With increasing age, stride length and walking speed decreased, while stance and double support phases increased (
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">p</jats:italic>
                      trend < 0.001). High-risk individuals showed shorter stride lengths, slower walking speeds, and longer stance phases than low-risk counterparts (
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">p</jats:italic>
                      < 0.05). Height-adjusted stride length correlated with Fall Risk Assessment components (r = 0.36,
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">p</jats:italic>
                      < 0.001), and those in the shortest quartile had over eightfold higher odds of high fall risk.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Height-adjusted stride length indicates fall risk.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Age-Related Differences in Gait Parameters and Their Association With Fall Risk in Older Adults: A Cross-Sectional Study

                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Suicidal ideation (SI) in nursing homes remains underexplored. This study examined whether meaning in life mediates associations between social vulnerability, perceived burdensomeness, and SI.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This is a cross-sectional study with 231 residents from Valencian Community, Spain, aged 60 years or older with preserved or mildly impaired cognitive functioning. Structural equation modeling tested direct and indirect associations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Lower meaning in life was associated with higher SI. Perceived burdensomeness and low social support were not directly associated with SI but were indirectly associated through reduced meaning in life, explaining 42.8% of its variance. Loneliness was directly associated with SI, whereas its association with low meaning in life was borderline.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Meaning in life may play a relevant role in the psychosocial factors examined and SI, although longitudinal research is needed. Interventions enhancing meaning and addressing loneliness may improve suicide prevention in nursing homes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Social Vulnerability and Suicidal Ideation in Nursing Home Residents: The Mediating Role of Meaning in Life

                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Older adults in long-term care facilities (LTCFs) faced social and care disruptions during COVID-19, but evidence on mental health burden and vulnerability remains fragmented.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To synthesise evidence on mental health outcomes among LTCF residents during the pandemic and identify resident- and facility-level vulnerability and protective conditions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>MEDLINE, Embase and PsycINFO were searched for English-language peer-reviewed studies published from January 2020 to January 2025. Findings were narratively synthesised, and exploratory random-effects meta-analyses were conducted where at least three studies reported extractable resident-level prevalence.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Thirty-two studies were included as follows: 24 quantitative, six qualitative and two mixed-methods. Most reported high prevalence, deterioration, or qualitative evidence of depression, anxiety, loneliness, isolation, or related distress. Pooled prevalence was 55.6% for depression, 51.4% for anxiety and 54.5% for loneliness, with substantial heterogeneity. Vulnerability reflected clinical, social and facility-level factors; consistent staffing, social connection and family communication were potential protective conditions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Mental Health Burden and Vulnerability Among Long-Term Care Facility Residents During the COVID-19 Pandemic: A Systematic Review With Exploratory Prevalence Meta-Analysis

                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To examine whether chair-rise difficulty functions as a functional mediator in the association between loneliness/social isolation and incident osteoarthritis (OA).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Data from 6,232 adults ≥50 in 12 European countries (SHARE waves 7–9, 2017–2022). Social isolation and loneliness were exposures; depression, physical inactivity, and chair-rise difficulty were mediators; OA onset was the outcome. Structural equation modeling tested mediation, adjusting for covariates.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>No direct associations were found; both exposures had significant indirect effects via depression and functional decline. Chair-rise difficulty was the strongest mediator (β = 0.74, p < 0.001), followed by depression (β = 0.04, p = 0.033). Physical inactivity acted indirectly through chair-rise difficulty (β = 0.26, p < 0.001). Female sex and older-age independently increased OA incidence.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Loneliness and social isolation were indirectly linked to incident OA via psychological, behavioral, and functional mechanisms. Chair-rise difficulty is a functional intermediary linking psychosocial distress to physical vulnerability and increased OA incidence, not a direct cause of joint-degeneration.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Chair-Rise Difficulty as a Functional Correlate in the Longitudinal Association Between Loneliness and Incident Osteoarthritis in Older Adults

                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Intergenerational support plays a crucial role in mental health in later life, yet both the heterogeneity of support patterns and the symptom-level interplay among depressive symptoms remain underexplored.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Using data from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS 2020,
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">N</jats:italic>
                      = 7,444), Latent Class Analysis (LCA) identified intergenerational support patterns. Network analysis and the Network Comparison Test (NCT) were utilized to estimate and compare depressive symptom networks (CESD-10) across subgroups.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Three patterns emerged: Distant-Supportive (55.9%), Proximate-Interactive (24.2%), and Traditional Co-resident (19.9%). While “sadness” and “being bothered” were universal core symptoms, NCT revealed distinct structural disparities. The Proximate-Interactive group exhibited a uniquely strong “bothered–fearful” connection. The Distant-Supportive group showed pronounced “effort–cannot get going” pathways, whereas the Traditional Co-resident group displayed a stronger “bothered–trouble focusing” link.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Intergenerational support patterns are not only associated with overall depression severity but also with differences in the network topology of depressive symptoms. Differentiated interventions tailored to specific family structures are essential for geriatric mental health.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Network Analysis of Depressive Symptoms Among Chinese Older Adults Across Different Intergenerational Support Patterns

                    <jats:p>Turnover among non-nursing staff such as housekeeping, dietary, laundry, and maintenance workers is a growing concern in nursing homes. Because these workers are essential to daily services for older adults, understanding their turnover trends is critical.</jats:p>

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We used turnover data from all Iowa nursing homes from 2009 to 2022 to summarize annual turnover rates and examine trends over time, stratified by profit status, rurality, and overall quality.</jats:p>

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The sample included 421 nursing homes with 5,130 facility-year observations. Turnover increased over time for all staff types; in 2022, turnover rates were 88.1% for housekeeping, 87.8% for dietary, 53.9% for laundry, and 43.6% for maintenance. Turnover was higher in for-profit, urban, and lower-quality facilities.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Non-nursing staff turnover in nursing homes is extremely high. Broader data collection is needed to evaluate its impact on quality.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

records.abstract: <jats:p>Background: Family co-residence is often considered protective for older adults in India but may not ensure inclusion in household decisions. This study examined how widowhood and decision-making exclusion are jointly associated with depressive symptoms among co-resident older adults. Methods: Data came from LASI Wave 1 (2017–18) and included 27,840 married or widowed adults aged 60+. Survey-weighted logistic regression examined widowhood, decision-making exclusion, their interaction, dose-response patterns, and sex-stratified associations with CES-D depressive symptoms. Results: Decision-making exclusion was highest among widowed women and lowest among married men. More extensive exclusion was associated with higher depressive symptoms, while widowhood without exclusion was not significant after full adjustment. There was little evidence that widowhood and exclusion interacted. Associations with depressive symptoms were more clearly observed among women than men. Conclusion: Among co-resident older adults, having a meaningful voice in family decisions may be important for mental health beyond shared residence alone.</jats:p>
title: Family Decision-Making Exclusion, Widowhood, and Depressive Symptoms Among Co-Resident Older Adults in India

records.abstract: <jats:p>We examine racial disparities in the association between work discrimination and life satisfaction among older adults and whether any differences are mediated by one’s sense of personal mastery using data from the 2010 and 2012 waves of the Health and Retirement Study. The results from the structural equation models (SEM) show White people who experience work discrimination report the lowest life satisfaction, followed by Hispanic and then Black people. After accounting for the mediating effect of one’s sense of mastery to cope with discriminatory work experiences, we find work discrimination still has a direct negative association with the life satisfaction of White and Black respondents but the effect for Hispanic people is no longer statistically significant. The results of the direct and total effects also suggest the mediating effects of mastery on the association between work discrimination and life satisfaction among older workers is strongest for White people, followed by Hispanic people and then Black people. These findings suggest that a person’s efficiency at drawing upon their coping resources like mastery when needed is essential for protecting their well-being from the harmful effects of work discrimination, especially for Black and Hispanic people.</jats:p>
title: Mastery as a Mediator for the Effects of Work Discrimination on Racial Disparities in Life Satisfaction

records.abstract: <jats:p>This study examined discrepancies between persons living with dementia (PLWD) and their spousal caregivers in the perceived importance of PLWD’s care needs, and how caregivers’ dementia knowledge and empathy were associated with these discrepancies. Data were drawn from 65 couples managing early-stage Alzheimer’s disease. PLWD self-reported the importance of their physical, psychological, and social needs, while caregivers provided proxy ratings. PLWD perceived addressing their physical needs as more important than did their caregivers, whereas both partners agreed on the importance of psychological and social needs. Caregivers’ greater empathic concern was associated with smaller discrepancies in the perceived importance of physical needs; greater personal distress was associated with smaller discrepancies in social needs. Caregivers’ dementia knowledge was positively associated with discrepancies in psychological needs only when relationship quality was lower. These findings highlight the importance of caregivers’ emotional responsiveness and relational dynamics in caregiver interventions, expanding the focus beyond dementia knowledge.</jats:p>
title: Spousal Discrepancy in Perceived Importance of Care Needs Among Couples Managing Early-Stage Alzheimer’s Disease

records.abstract: <jats:p>We examined associations between sexual activity, sexual quality, and glycosylated hemoglobin (HbA1c) levels among partnered older adults with diabetes. Using longitudinal data from the National Social Life, Health, and Aging Project, we studied 620 partnered respondents with diabetes aged 57 to 85 at baseline. We estimated mixed-effects models of sexual activity, frequency, and quality on HbA1c trajectories over ten years, including tests for gender differences. Results indicated that being sexually active and having sex a few times a month were associated with more favorable HbA1c trajectories compared to being sexually inactive. Emotional satisfaction was associated with worsening HbA1c trajectories for women but stable trajectories for men. Physical pleasure showed no gender differences. The findings suggest that partnered sexuality is a meaningful, gendered aspect of older adults’ metabolic health that deserves greater attention as a dimension of diabetes care in later life.</jats:p>
title: Sexuality and Glycosylated Hemoglobin Levels in Partnered Older Adults With Diabetes

records.abstract: <jats:p>This study investigates how retirement’s effect on subsequent health varies by individual attributes and their interaction. Instead of spotlighting heterogeneity for a specific, theoretically predetermined feature, I consider the feature-wide effect heterogeneity to find possible data-driven candidates that generate this heterogeneity. To accomplish this, I use causal forests and harmonized data from the Gateway to Global Aging Data (the Gateway). The results show that temporal dimensions (such as age and birth cohort) and financial dimensions (such as income and wealth) are the most important features in heterogenizing retirement’s effect on health. Based on these findings, I suggest the “double scaffold” model to comprehensively explain feature-wide effect heterogeneity.</jats:p>
title: Double Scaffold of Retirement on Subsequent Health: Revisiting Spatio-Temporality and Finance Through the Feature-Wide Effect Heterogeneity

records.abstract: <jats:p>More than 60% of older workers report experiencing ageism in the workplace, yet little is known about whether the relationship between ageism, job satisfaction, and mental health differs by US-born status. This study examined whether job satisfaction mediates the association between workplace ageism and depressive symptoms and assessed whether this association differs by US-born status. Data were drawn from the 2018 and 2020 National Longitudinal Survey of Youth 1979 for workers aged 53- 62, and a multiple-group path analysis was conducted. The results indicated that, among US-born workers, job satisfaction significantly mediated the associations between depressive symptoms and both ageism in promotion and ageism in early retirement. Among immigrant workers, however, this mediating effect was significant only for ageism in promotion. Findings underscore the importance of developing anti-ageism policies that adopt an intersectional approach, jointly considering US-born status and age to reduce the detrimental impacts of ageism on workers’ mental health.</jats:p>
title: Workplace Ageism, Job Satisfaction, and Depressive Symptoms Among Older Workers: The Roles of US-Born Status

records.abstract: <jats:p>As populations age and the share of retirees increases across Europe, the question of whether individuals stay active after retirement is increasingly salient. Retirees are known to provide more instrumental support than their working counterparts. However, most previous studies have relied on between-group comparisons of retirees and employed individuals, leaving it unclear how the transition into retirement affects changes in instrumental support within individuals over time. Using eight waves of the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe covering 19 countries between 2004–2022 (n = 7,422 observations from 3,711 individuals aged 50+), we employed fixed-effects regression and found that the transition from employment to retirement was associated with an increase in instrumental support provision outside the household. We also found suggestive evidence that this association was stronger in countries with higher social expenditures. These findings indicate that retirement may promote activity and facilitate engagement in helping others.</jats:p>
title: Changes in Instrumental Support Around Retirement: Longitudinal Evidence From Europe

records.abstract: <jats:p>Older adults who need community services may remain uncertain whether those services are locally provided or judge that they are not. Research on perceived unmet need often combines these positions. Using a cross-sectional survey of 929 adults aged 60 or older in urban Jiangsu, China, we paired reported need with perceived provision across 20 services and distinguished awareness gaps, perceived non-provision, and comparison uncertainty for services not reported as needed. Fractional logit models examined associations with social participation and functional status. Greater social participation was associated with fewer awareness gaps, concentrated among adults with ADL disability (−8.75 percentage points per SD). A weaker, less stable association with perceived non-provision appeared among functionally independent adults, and no counterpart appeared for comparison uncertainty. Unresolved uncertainty and negative provision judgments may call for different responses, and outreach may be especially relevant for older adults with ADL disability.</jats:p>
title: Need-Conditioned Uncertainty and Perceived Non-Provision of Community Services: Social Participation and Functional Status Among Older Adults in Urban China

records.abstract: <jats:p>The Johns Hopkins Undergraduate Summer Training and Research Program (Hopkins USTAR) was a 2-year program funded by the National Institute on Aging R25 Advancing Diversity in Aging Research through Undergraduate Education. Hopkins USTAR was designed to provide undergraduate students primarily from underrepresented backgrounds in biomedical and behavioral science with interdisciplinary research training in aging and health disparities research. From 2023 to 2025, a total of 15 undergraduate students participated in faculty-mentored research projects, professional development, research education, and national research conferences. Program evaluation methods included pre- and post-program surveys and interviews. Results suggest that the Hopkins USTAR program significantly increased aspects of participants’ research self-efficacy and strengthened perceived science identity. Despite the early termination of Hopkins USTAR, the program's short-term outcomes indicate modest success in fostering positive feelings about science and preparing participants for graduate school. Continued follow-up to assess long-term program outcomes will be important to measure impact.</jats:p>

records.abstract: <jats:p>Psychotherapeutic interventions can support people with dementia. Family members often play a pivotal role in the therapeutic process but little is known about their experiences of therapy, how they perceive the impact on their relative, and how the experience affects them directly. This study aimed to explore the experiences of family members who engage in therapy, or support someone living with dementia to attend therapy. Individuals with dementia and their family members were recruited as participants through NHS Trusts, professional networks, social media and community and support groups based in England and Wales. Semi-structured qualitative individual or dyadic interviews were conducted with 17 participants, eight of whom were living with dementia and nine were family members. Framework analysis was used. Family members highlighted “the importance of feeling seen” as distinct individuals by clinicians when engaging with psychotherapy, and not just the carer of their partner. When working with “dementia as dynamic phenomenon”, therapeutic approaches needed to balance being sufficiently structured and containing whilst allowing for adaptions to each individual changeable presentation. Participants highlighted how psychotherapy presented “expected and unexpected outcomes”, challenges that arose when outcomes were not agreed upon, and how therapy functioned as a support structure in ways the participants did not foresee. Psychotherapeutic intervention provides meaningful support to the family members of individuals with dementia. Understanding the needs of family members, alongside the needs of the individual with dementia, and taking a systemic approach is conducive to better therapeutic outcomes. The changeable nature of dementia presentation means that a therapeutic approach should be flexible based on the needs of the family. Psychotherapeutic intervention with individuals with dementia can have a range of benefits for the individual and the wider family, when sufficient considerations are made to understand each person’s needs.</jats:p>
title: The Experiences of Psychotherapy for People With Dementia: A Qualitative Interview Study With Family Members

records.abstract: <jats:p>Person-centered care (PCC) is the gold standard for improving the quality of life (QoL) of people living with dementia. The Montessori method represents a practical model for implementing PCC in Nursing Homes (NHs). To date, no study has documented how residents describe their QoL in NHs implementing this method using a self-report approach consistent with PCC principles. This study explores residents’ perceptions of their QoL, as well as how they relate it to the care model, using a qualitative self-assessment tool. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with twenty-nine residents from two NHs with high levels of Montessori implementation assessed using a validated tool. All interviews were analyzed using thematic analysis. Three interconnected themes emerged. The first examines the components of QoL that matter most to residents. The second explores how the care model influences these determinants. Finally, the third describes residents’ self-assessment of QoL shaped by individual factors. Our study contributes to a better understanding of the Montessori method as a comprehensive PCC model from residents’ perspectives and deepens knowledge of the extent to which it can shape their QoL. These findings also provide practical and methodological insights for evaluating QoL and guiding care models promoting QoL.</jats:p>
title: Exploring Quality of Life Through Residents’ Voice in Nursing Homes: A Qualitative Study of a Montessori-Based Person-Centered Model of Care

records.abstract: <jats:p>Purpose: People with dementia can and do live successfully on their own, but there are additional challenges for people living alone without informal support. This paper reports findings of the first study in the UK to examine needs and experiences of, and services for, people with dementia who live alone without informal support. Method: The study involved a service audit of 13 local authority commissioners in two English regions, interviews with 22 people with dementia who live alone without informal carers, and case studies of four services supporting this group. Findings: Awareness of this population among commissioners was limited. There were very few services which explicitly supported this group, and some mainstream services excluded people without carers. None of the local authorities collected data on numbers of people with dementia living alone, or those without informal support, in their area. Some participants with dementia had contacted social care, but this had not always resulted in appropriate support, and people reported problematic interactions with staff, assumptions that friends would provide care, and support not being available at the right time. Self-funders were left with little support. People with dementia were resourceful, using general services, technology, and other tactics, including cleaners, meal delivery, community taxis, and automatic reminders to organise their lives. However, as many of these additional services have a cost attached, there is potential to exacerbate existing inequalities. Participants wanted more support, particularly with finances and administrative tasks. Services can help this group with supported handovers, allowing self-referral back into a service, and keeping case files open. Conclusions: Both the number of people with dementia, and the number of people ageing without children, are rising, and it will therefore become increasingly important to facilitate effective support for people with dementia to live independently without informal support.</jats:p>
title: Living Alone With Dementia: Managing Without Informal Support to Contact and Navigate Services

records.abstract: <jats:p>The aim of this study was to gain insight into young dementia carer-specific content provided on the websites of dementia and (young) carers organizations in seven European countries including: the UK, the Netherlands, Italy, Greece, Portugal, Ireland and Sweden. Research questions were: 1). What types of young dementia carer-specific content are available on national websites of dementia and (young) carers organizations across Europe? and 2). How does the content address the complex impact that dementia can have on young dementia carers? The identification of websites was informed by the contextual characteristics of each country in relation to dementia and young carers support and services. A standard protocol describing the website inclusion and exclusion criteria, data extraction and content analysis using a categorical coding framework was followed. Descriptive statistics were calculated to summarize data within and across countries. A total of 312 organizations with active websites meeting the eligibility criteria across countries were identified, and their websites reviewed. Content relevant to young dementia carers was identified in 28% (n = 86) of the websites, with uneven availability of resources across Europe and very limited resources in some countries. Most contents addressed five categories: Diagnosis & symptoms, Uncertainty & family distress, Changes in roles, Stigma & isolation and Identifying need for support. A lack of tailored resources to support young dementia carers was identified, particularly in relation to two categories: Grief & loss and Education & life planning. Only a minority of websites included young dementia carer-specific content. These websites primarily focused on general support needs and explanations of dementia, while key areas such as guidance on school, career, and life planning remain underdeveloped. There is a need for greater recognition of young dementia carers, clearer terminology, and more developmentally appropriate and practically oriented resources to strengthen online support for these carers across Europe.</jats:p>
title: Content Analysis of Free Online Information and Support Available to Young Dementia Carers Across Europe

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Spirituality is a core component of person-centred dementia care, yet spiritual needs may be under-recognised as cognition and communication decline. Spiritual Reminiscence Therapy (SRT) is a structured intervention that emphasises meaning-making and existential reflection rather than autobiographical recall alone. We examined the clinical outcomes and implementation characteristics of SRT in older adults with dementia.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A scoping review was conducted using Arksey and O’Malley’s framework and reported in accordance with PRISMA Extension for Scoping Reviews guidelines. Electronic databases (Cochrane, EMBASE, MEDLINE, PubMed and PsycINFO) were searched from inception to 26 December 2025, supplemented by grey literature and reference screening. Eligible English-language quantitative and qualitative studies evaluating SRT in adults aged ≥65 years with dementia were included. Data were synthesised descriptively.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Four studies met inclusion criteria (2 qualitative, 1 randomized controlled trial, 1 prospective cohort study). SRT was associated with improvements in spiritual well-being, life meaning and hope. Psychological outcomes suggested increased life satisfaction and reduced depressive symptoms. Qualitative findings indicated enhanced social connectedness in residential care settings. Evidence for cognitive benefit was inconsistent and clinically modest, and functional outcomes were rarely assessed. Reporting of intervention delivery and implementation processes was variable.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>SRT may improve meaning-related and depressive symptoms in persons with dementia, however extant evidence is limited and methodologically heterogenous. Future research prioritizing standardised outcomes, longer follow-up and formal implementation evaluation are needed before broader integration into routine psychogeriatric practice.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Spiritual Reminiscence Therapy for Older Persons With Dementia: A Scoping Review

<jats:p>This study aimed to assess the recorded prevalence of a dementia diagnosis and the receipt of appropriate dementia care among current Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander clients of Aboriginal and Community Controlled Health Services (ACCHS) aged 45 and over, as documented in medical records. ACCHSs are Australian primary healthcare organisations that are initiated, governed and operated by local Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities. A manual audit of medical records was undertaken by a staff member from each participating ACCHS to identify current clients with a documented diagnosis of dementia and examine their receipt of key elements of dementia-related care. Across 9 ACCHSs located in New South Wales, a total of 70 clients with a recorded diagnosis of dementia were identified (1.2% recorded prevalence rate). The majority of clients with a dementia diagnosis had documented receipt of elements of appropriate dementia care including an active chronic disease management plan (61%), annual health assessment (56%), referral to aged care services (69%), and assessment of one or more dementia-related risks (94%). However, less than half of clients had a documented cognitive assessment within the last 12 months (41%) or completed any advance planning documentation (37%). Clients with a dementia diagnosis received a mean of 3.6 out of 6 assessed elements of best practice dementia care. As with primary care nationally and internationally, ACCHSs require co-designed support strategies to enhance their processes for dementia diagnosis and documentation and to build upon their delivery of best-practice dementia care. Priority dementia care areas for older clients with a confirmed dementia diagnosis include the evaluation of dementia-related risks such as elder abuse and driving safety, and the implementation of advance care planning including discussion or completion of relevant legal documents.</jats:p>

                    Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry (
                    <jats:ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" ext-link-type="uri" xlink:href="https://anzctr.org.au/">https://anzctr.org.au/</jats:ext-link>

title: The Prevalence of Dementia Diagnosis and Delivery of Appropriate Dementia Care in Aboriginal Community Controlled Health Services

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Motor dysfunction is associated with cognitive vulnerability, but whether impairments across body regions jointly contribute to motoric cognitive risk syndrome (MCR) remains unclear. We examined the independent and joint associations of handgrip strength and chair-stand test (CST) with MCR.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This cross-sectional study included 6258 dementia-free older adults (mean age 71.5 ± 6.6 years; 63.1% women) from a community-based cohort. Handgrip strength and CST performance were used to define upper- and lower-extremity motor impairment. Participants were classified as normal, handgrip weakness only, CST impairment only, or combined motor impairment. Multivariable logistic regression was performed with adjustment for demographic, socioeconomic, lifestyle, and clinical factors. Additive and multiplicative interactions were assessed.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>MCR was present in 10.4% of participants. Using the A/B CST cutoff as the primary definition, adjusted odds ratios (95% confidence intervals) for MCR, compared with normal function, were 1.84 (1.14–2.97) for handgrip weakness only, 4.17 (2.97–5.85) for CST impairment only, and 9.17 (6.56–12.81) for combined motor impairment. Associations were directionally consistent across alternative CST cutoffs. A positive additive interaction was observed at the A/B CST cutoff (relative excess risk due to interaction = 3.48; attributable proportion = 0.40; and synergy index = 1.83), whereas multiplicative interaction was not positive.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Combined handgrip weakness and poorer CST performance were strongly associated with prevalent MCR. A positive additive interaction at the primary CST cutoff suggests that joint motor impairment may help characterize MCR-related vulnerability in older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Joint associations of handgrip strength and chair-stand performance with motoric cognitive risk syndrome in older adults

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Acute decompensated heart failure (ADHF) is the most common cause of hospitalization in older adults. Cellular senescence, a hallmark of aging biology, has been implicated in heart failure pathophysiology and functional decline via the pro-inflammatory senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP). We evaluated the association between SASP and physical function in older adults hospitalized for ADHF.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>REHAB-HF was a trial of older adults hospitalized for ADHF randomized to a novel physical rehabilitation intervention or attention control. We measured a panel of 18-SASP analytes at in-hospital baseline and at 3-month follow-up. Outcomes included short physical performance battery (SPPB) and 6-minute walk distance (6MWD). Statistical analysis included principal component analysis (PCA) of log- and z-transformed SASP values. Associations were evaluated with multivariable regression models adjusted for age, sex, and intervention arm.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Samples were available for 226 (65%) of the REHAB-HF participants with mean age (SD) 72.3 (8), 53% female, 52% HFpEF, and 53% assigned to rehab intervention. Principal Component 1 (PC1) reflected a coordinated signal across biomarkers of inflammation and immune signaling. PC1 was associated with poorer function at baseline [(SPPB -0.46 [-0.77, -0.14]; p = 0.004 and 6MWD -19.7 meters [-32.7, -6.7]; p = 0.003)]. Increasing SASP over time was associated with clinically significant reduced physical function improvement (ΔSPPB -1.80 [-2.58, -1.03]; p &lt; 0.001 and Δ6MWD -49.7 meters [-77.2, -22.1]; p = 0.001).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Higher SASP levels were associated with poorer physical function recovery in older patients hospitalized for ADHF. These findings suggest that inflammatory SASP biomarkers may improve risk stratification and potentially guide therapeutic strategies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>REHAB-HF trial is registered at clinicaltrials.gov Clinical Trial Registry</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>NCT02196038</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Senescence Biomarkers Predict Physical Function and Clinical Outcomes After Heart Failure Hospitalization: Insights From REHAB-HF

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Epigenetic aging algorithms are emerging tools for understanding the biological effects of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). A growing body of literature has applied DNA methylation-based epigenetic clocks in people living with HIV (PWH) across the life course, examining epigenetic age acceleration (EAA) in relation to HIV infection, antiretroviral therapy (ART), comorbidities, and clinical biomarkers (e.g., viral load, CD4 T-cell counts). This systematic review (Prospero: CRD420251126874) summarizes and synthesizes the current evidence on epigenetic aging in PWH across the life course and identifies critical knowledge gaps for future research. We searched PubMed, Scopus, and Medline through June 26, 2026. The review followed PRISMA guidelines and assessed studies for risk of bias using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. We created a narrative synthesis of results and performed a random-effects meta-analysis of HorvathAge EAA. Fifty-five studies met the inclusion criteria. More than half (n = 33) examined EAA in PWH compared to an uninfected control population. We identified heterogeneity in study populations and design, biospecimens profiled, platforms used for DNA methylation analysis, and epigenetic clocks employed. Only 6 studies included participants younger than 18 years and no studies focused exclusively on individuals over 65 years. Only 10 studies examined longitudinal changes in EAA. Thirty-seven papers evaluated associations between EAA and comorbidities. A meta-analysis of HorvathAge EAA across 14 studies found a mean difference of 3.41 years (95%CI 2.22, 4.60) in PWH relative to controls. Current evidence supports accelerated EAA among PWH but highlights substantial methodological heterogeneity and important knowledge gaps. Longitudinal studies of EAA in PWH are needed in populations under 18 and over 65, to clarify the effects of ART, clinical biomarkers, and age-related comorbidities, and determine the clinical utility of epigenetic aging biomarkers.</jats:p>
title: Epigenetic aging in people with HIV across the life course: a systematic review and meta-analysis

records.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>As populations age, most deaths occur in people with multiple long-term conditions (MLTC). When decline is driven by coexisting conditions, the palliative phase and associated needs often go unrecognised. Improving palliative care for this group is an international priority, yet no recent review has described their needs at the end of life.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To map the extent, range and nature of evidence on the palliative care needs of people with MLTC and their family caregivers, describe its characteristics and identify knowledge gaps.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Scoping review of quantitative, qualitative and mixed-methods primary studies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Eligibility criteria</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Adults aged ≥50 years with ≥2 long-term conditions plus indicators of advanced disease or poor prognosis. Single-condition studies, early-stage MLTC, non-disaggregated data, disease-modifying interventions and non-primary research were excluded.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Sources of Evidence</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, Scopus and PsycINFO, searched from inception to 8 September 2025.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Charting Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Records were dual-screened and charted by design, setting and established conceptual frameworks of domains of need.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Of 7568 records, 90 studies were included. Four domains were identified: (i) comprehensive support needs in the context of functional decline; (ii) proactive care needs shaped by limited death literacy and prognostic uncertainty; (iii) systems-level needs for coordination and collaboration; and (iv) compounded needs arising from inequality (diagnostic/sociodemographic).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Older adults with MLTC face complex, often unmet needs, requiring support for functional decline, equitable proactive care, coordinated systems and improved death literacy. Palliative care must be integrated, responsive to MLTC realities and guided by what matters most to patients and caregivers.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: The palliative care needs of people with multiple long-term conditions and their family caregivers: a scoping review of mixed study designs

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Polypharmacy is common in people living with dementia (PLwD) and associated with adverse outcomes. Although Structured Medication Reviews (SMRs) are recommended to optimise medication regimens, their delivery is often constrained by limited resources. Artificial intelligence (AI) may support SMRs, yet little is known about how it is perceived by PLwD and their carers. This study explored their experiences of polypharmacy, views on SMRs and attitudes towards use of AI tools in SMRs.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Semi-structured interviews with 12 PLwD experiencing polypharmacy and two focus groups with 14 carers were conducted via Microsoft Teams or telephone and analysed using Reflexive Thematic Analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Two themes were constructed: participants’ perspectives on meaningful SMRs, and embracing AI while preserving patient safety and the human touch. Participants described challenges in managing polypharmacy, with carers playing a central role in supporting adherence and monitoring side effects. Experiences of SMRs varied. SMRs were most valued when clinicians were empathetic and able to offer personalised guidance. Participants viewed AI use in SMRs positively, provided that such tools were well validated and used to assist rather than replace healthcare professionals. AI was also seen as potentially reducing administrative burden and supporting more person-centred care. However, some had concerns regarding patient safety and data security, highlighting the need for appropriate regulation and human oversight.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Participants were supportive of AI use in SMRs, despite concerns about safety, data security and disclosure of AI use, and emphasised the importance of patient-clinician interactions and lived experience involvement in AI tool development.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Attitudes of people living with dementia and their carers towards the use of generative artificial intelligence to inform structured medication reviews

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To improve the implementation and uptake of a multifactorial falls prevention intervention, the Belgian Program to Enhance the Uptake and Effectiveness of a Multifactorial Falls Prevention Intervention in Community-Dwelling Older people (BE-EMPOWERed) program was systematically developed. It includes a 7-week group program for older people, workshops for healthcare professionals and an implementation plan with implementation guidance for primary care areas (PCAs) in Flanders. This study implemented BE-EMPOWERed in four PCAs and evaluated its implementation processes and implementation outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This embedded mixed-methods process evaluation was conducted over a 2-year period in four PCAs. Implementation processes and outcomes were assessed using participant lists, fidelity checklists, observations, focus group interviews and self-reported intervention costs. The process evaluation was guided by the Medical Research Council framework. Quantitative data were analysed descriptively and qualitative data were analysed using the Qualitative Analysis Guide of Leuven.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A total of 196 people participated in the group program with high attendance across sessions. Fidelity assessments across 20 group programs demonstrated high adherence to many structural and delivery-related program components. However, lower fidelity was observed for some behaviour change components. Qualitative findings suggested increased knowledge and awareness among older people, with reported application of falls prevention interventions in daily life. Overall, the findings indicate that strong engagement stemmed from group dynamics and the way group leaders delivered the program, while sustainability was hindered by limited resources and reliance on local champions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The BE-EMPOWERed program was feasible and acceptable across diverse PCAs, with high engagement and overall good fidelity. However, challenges in sustainability highlight the need for structural support to enable long-term implementation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Study protocol</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT06105437).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
