<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Polypharmacy and potentially inappropriate medications (PIMs) are common in older adults, but the prevalence in those with a prognosis of 6 months or less is poorly characterised. We estimated the prevalence of polypharmacy, PIMs and potential prescribing omissions (PPOs) in older adults approaching end of life.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We systematically searched six databases from inception to 30 April 2026, for studies reporting polypharmacy (≥5 medications) or PIMs in adults aged ≥65 years with life-limiting illnesses (≤6-month prognosis). Two reviewers independently screened records, extracted data and assessed bias using Joanna Briggs Institute or Newcastle-Ottawa tools. Pooled prevalence used random-effects models. Heterogeneity was explored by setting, region and assessment tool. The review was registered with PROSPERO (CRD42023454636).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Eighteen studies (499 853 participants, 52.3% female) were included in this review. Pooled prevalence of polypharmacy was 76% (95% CI 65%–87%) with excessive polypharmacy (≥10 medications) at 34% (9%–58%). PIM prevalence was high at 54% (40%–68%), and remained above 50% until the final week of life, with preventive medications (statins, antithrombotics, proton pump inhibitors) often continued until death. Substantial heterogeneity was present in all pooled analyses (I2 &gt; 99%), highlighting considerable variability across studies. Only two studies assessed PPOs 30% lacked prophylactic laxatives with opioids while 76.6% lacked strong opioids for moderate–severe cancer pain.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Interpretation</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Polypharmacy and PIMs use are highly prevalent among people with limited life prognosis, suggesting that evidence-based deprescribing protocols are needed for this vulnerable population. Nevertheless, this needs to be taken in light of the substantial heterogeneity of PIM definitions, underscoring the need for standardised PIM assessment in this population.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Prevalence of polypharmacy and potentially inappropriate prescribing in older adults with a prognosis of 6 months or less: a systematic review and meta-analysis

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Bedridden older people generally have poor comprehensive capacity and are prone to multi-system complications including pressure injuries and lower limb venous thrombosis, imposing heavy caregiving and financial burdens and severely affecting their health.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To identify distinct trajectories of ability in bedridden older people and characteristics distinguishing the trajectories, while assessing the prognostic value of these trajectories for early risk identification of pressure injury and deep-vein thrombosis (DVT).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Participants</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Two hundred twenty six bedridden older people aged 65 years and above from two nursing homes in China.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Patients were required 5 assessments during 1-year follow-up period. Latent Growth Mixture Modelling identified distinct trajectories, multinomial logistic regression identified characteristics distinguishing the trajectories and generalised estimating equations evaluated associations between trajectories and pressure injury and DVT.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>There are three distinct trajectories of comprehensive capacity among bedridden older people, including severe impairment with stable type (63.5%); moderate impairment with slowly deteriorating type (16.3%); moderate-to-severe impairment with fluctuating type (20.2%). Characteristics distinguishing the trajectories were tooth loss, hypertension, indwelling gastric tube and dysphagia. Compared with the severe impairment stable type, the other two groups had higher pressure injury risk; the moderate impairment with slowly deteriorating type also had higher DVT risk.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Capacity trajectories of bedridden older people are heterogeneous. Nurses may want to focus on those with tooth loss, hypertension, indwelling gastric tube and dysphagia to deliver targeted care. These trajectories are significantly associated with pressure injury and deep vein thrombosis risks. Their identification enables earlier risk stratification and more targeted prevention.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: The trajectories of comprehensive capacity of bedridden older people based on latent growth mixture models: a longitudinal study

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Muscle strength is a well-established indicator of overall health, yet its prospective association with the incidence and prognosis of venous thromboembolism (VTE) remains inconsistent.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This prospective cohort study included 481 945 participants without prior VTE from the UK Biobank for incidence analysis, and 14 908 patients with prevalent VTE at baseline for prognostic analysis. Muscle strength was assessed using grip strength relative to body weight and categorised into sex- and age-specific tertiles. Cox proportional hazards models were used to estimate hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for incident VTE and all-cause mortality.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Over a median follow-up of 13.72 years, 15 774 incident VTE events were documented. Each 1-standard deviation increase in muscle strength was associated with a 13% reduction in VTE risk (HR 0.87, 95% CI: 0.85–0.89). Compared with the low muscle strength group, participants in the middle and high tertiles had 12% (HR 0.88, 95% CI: 0.84–0.92) and 19% (HR 0.81, 95% CI: 0.77–0.84) lower risk of VTE. This inverse association remained consistent across all genetic risk strata. Among patients with VTE, 2884 deaths occurred during follow-up. Each 1-standard deviation increase was associated with a 14% lower mortality risk (HR 0.86, 95% CI: 0.82–0.90). High and middle muscle strength were associated with 21% (HR 0.79, 95% CI: 0.72–0.87) and 17% (HR 0.83, 95% CI: 0.76–0.91) lower all-cause mortality versus low strength.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Higher muscle strength is associated with a lower risk of incident VTE, regardless of genetic predisposition, and with lower mortality among patients with VTE.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Association of muscle strength with the incidence of venous thromboembolism and all-cause mortality among patients: a prospective cohort study

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To examine associations between amount of income support received and entry into long-term care facilities (LTCFs) among older income support recipients, by homeownership status.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A national retrospective cohort study was conducted. Individuals aged 65–105 years who received income support and had a first-time long-term care eligibility assessment in Australia between 01/01/2010 and 30/06/2021 were included. Associations between means-tested income support payments and rate of entry into LTCFs stratified by homeownership status were assessed using inverse probability of treatment weighted, cause-specific Cox proportional hazards models. Additional analyses included sex-specific analyses and sub-group analyses to examine associations for people with dementia.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In total, 633 253 people were included [56.2% (n = 355 917) female; median age 82 years (interquartile range 76–86); 17.8% (n = 112 724) living with dementia; 69.1% (n = 437 445) homeowners]. Higher levels of income support were associated with a higher rate of entry into LTCFs for both homeowners [hazard ratio (HR) highest quartile vs lowest quartile: 1.08; 95% confidence interval (CI): 1.06–1.10] and non-homeowners [HR 1.08; 95% CI 1.05–1.12]. Findings were consistent for males, but for females, only those with moderate income support (third quartile) had a higher rate of LTCF entry. The findings were similar when only including people with dementia.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Greater reliance on means-tested income support payments, a potential indicator of financial vulnerability in later life, was associated with a higher rate of entry into LTCFs among both homeowners and non-homeowners. The study findings also suggest a complex relationship between income support reliance later in life and LTCF entry among older females.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Associations between income support payments and entry to long-term care facilities: a national retrospective cohort study

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Effective implementation of guidelines into residential aged care facilities (RACFs) is important for high-quality care. The 12-month Evidence-based Medication knowledge Brokers in Residential Aged CarE (EMBRACE) helix–counterbalanced randomised controlled trial evaluated three strategies to implement Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Appropriate Use of Psychotropic Medications in People Living with Dementia and in Residential Aged Care: (i) passive distribution of Guideline material, (ii) pharmacist-led staff education and (iii) knowledge broker-led Guideline implementation. All three strategies reduced Guideline non-concordance over time, with no significant difference between strategies. This mixed-method process evaluation examined delivery of the implementation strategies, including contextual factors important for Guideline implementation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Semi-structured interviews conducted with 34 health and care professionals at 12 months were thematically analysed using a deductive approach informed by the Grant framework. Descriptive statistics summarised quantitative data from a post-trial survey completed by intervention pharmacists.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Distribution of Guideline materials occurred opportunistically with RACF staff preferring summary materials (e.g. one-page factsheets). Pharmacist-led staff education was tailored to be shorter, more frequent and delivered one-on-one or in small groups. Knowledge broker pharmacists spent a median 70% of time delivering quality improvement activities including audit and feedback and integrating psychotropic best practice into RACF procedures and digital systems. Facilitators of successful Guideline implementation included early engagement with aged care leadership and knowledge broker integration into the team.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Guideline implementation efforts in RACFs may benefit from a multifaceted implementation approach involving early engagement with aged care leadership and contextualised delivery of implementation strategies according to staff preferences and needs.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Mixed-method process evaluation of the Evidence-based Medication knowledge Brokers in Residential Aged CarE (EMBRACE) helix–counterbalanced randomised controlled trial

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Extreme heat is a major environmental threat to healthy ageing, with older people experiencing the highest rates of heat-related morbidity and mortality. Although age-related physiological changes, multimorbidity and frailty remain key determinants of heat susceptibility, climate change, social inequalities and energy insecurity are reshaping the conditions in which older people experience and respond to thermal stress. This narrative New Horizons review integrates evidence identified through a structured, non-systematic search of peer-reviewed literature and relevant institutional reports across geriatric medicine, environmental health and climate science. It examines how frailty, intrinsic capacity, housing, energy affordability and social frailty influence the ability of older people to recognise risk, access protection and respond effectively to extreme heat. Particular attention is given to energy insecurity and summer cooling poverty, through which limited access to affordable household energy may undermine resilience. Ageing models primarily characterise individual vulnerability and functioning within the environment, whereas climate vulnerability models organise risk around exposure, sensitivity and adaptation; we use adaptive capacity to connect these perspectives by asking whether personal and contextual resources can be mobilised for protection. It may provide a conceptual basis for developing and subsequently validating a heat-adapted comprehensive geriatric assessment and for informing targeted prevention and climate adaptation policies for ageing populations.</jats:p>
title: New horizons in adaptive capacity and heat-related health in older people: integrating frailty, energy insecurity and social resources

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD) serves as a model to study muscle plasticity and recovery. Exercise recovery declines with age, and while omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (n-3 PUFA) exhibit inconsistent effects in younger adults, the effect in older adults is unknown.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In a double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial, 43 healthy, older women and men (65-85 years) ingested 5 mL of n-3 PUFA algae oil (2 g PUFA) or placebo for eight weeks. After eight weeks participants performed a bout of 10 × 10 eccentric-emphasised leg extensions. Outcome measures included quadriceps maximal voluntary contraction (MVC), muscle soreness, creatine kinase (CK) and inflammation (Interleukin-6, high-sensitive C-reactive protein; CRP) assessed at baseline and post-exercise.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>EIMD symptoms such as muscle soreness and function were modest and consistent with previous reports in older adults. Overall, n-3 PUFA supplementation did not improve functional recovery. However, a borderline greater MVC loss was observed in the n-3 PUFA group (time × group: P = .064), which resulted from significantly lower MVC in the n-3 PUFA group at 24 h (difference: −10.9%, 95%CI: −21.4;−0.40%, P = .042) and at 72 h (difference: −9.80, 95%CI: −18.3;−1.27, P = .025) post-exercise compared to the placebo. No significant overall group differences were observed for CK, interleukin-6, CRP, but CK concentrations significantly increased from baseline at 24 h post-exercise in the placebo group (change: +81.1%, 95%CI:10.5;152%, P = .014). Habitual physical activity and sex emerged as significant moderators of molecular recovery in an exploratory analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>n-3 PUFA supplementation did not improve functional recovery, but different molecular response patterns were observed. Habitual physical activity and sex may be determinants of post-exercise response; this exploratory finding warrants confirmation in larger studies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Eight-week omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid supplementation alters but does not attenuate exercise-induced muscle damage in older adults: a randomised controlled trial

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Home hospital has been shown to achieve comparable, if not better, clinical and patient-centred outcomes compared to brick-and-mortar (BAM) hospitalisation. Family caregivers (FCs) play an essential role in delivering home hospital care; however, their perceptions towards the home hospital model remain an active area of inquiry, particularly in rural settings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We conducted a mixed methods analysis of FCs of patients participating in a multicenter randomised controlled trial of rural home hospital in the USA and Canada. We compared pre- and post-intervention burden among home hospital and BAM caregivers with the Zarit Burden Interview-12 (ZBI-12) scale (n = 20 home hospital, n = 10 BAM). We conducted semi-structured qualitative interviews with home hospital caregivers (n = 19). Qualitative data were coded and analysed using thematic analysis to construct core themes and subthemes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>There was no significant difference in median ZBI-12 scores between home hospital and BAM at admission (4 interquartile range [IQR 2–9.3] vs 5 [IQR 0.3–9.3]; P = .723), discharge (6 [3.3–8] vs 7.5 [2.5–11.8], P = .309), or change from admission to discharge (0 [−2.5 to 3] vs 1.5 [0–3.5]; P = .269). Our qualitative analysis revealed three central themes: (i) The caregiving experience was positively shaped by strong communication and shared decision-making with the care team; (ii) Caregivers described receiving high-quality home hospital care, particularly surrounding patient-centeredness and technology; and (iii) Home hospital was perceived to offer greater flexibility, comfort and psychosocial support compared to BAM hospitalisation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Home hospital provides numerous benefits for FCs without increasing perceived burden; further work is needed to establish potential supports to optimise their experience.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: The experience of family caregivers when their loved one is home hospitalized: a mixed methods analysis of a randomized controlled trial

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Interprofessional training is essential for high-quality care of older adults. Despite widespread recognition of its importance, evidence on perceived geriatric competence remains limited to studies on single countries or professions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Secondary analysis of a COST Action multinational multilingual web-based survey (PROmoting GeRiAtric Medicine in countries where it is still eMergING, PROGRAMMING) conducted across the 27 European Union Member States (EU-27) and non-EU-27 countries between 9 October 2023 and 5 June 2024. Four thousand seven hundred eighty-eight professionals from 10 core health and social care groups were included. We explored perceived Knowledge, Relevance and Interest across seven domains required for comprehensive geriatric assessment: frailty, falls and mobility, delirium, depression, mild cognitive impairment and dementia screening, nutritional assessment and malnutrition, polypharmacy and deprescribing. Student’s t test; one-way analysis of variance, hierarchical clustering and latent class analysis were used to identify interprofessional differences and shared patterns across professions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Mean age was 42.4 years (SD 11.9); 3432 (71.7%) were women; 2893 (60.4%) worked in EU-27 countries. Interprofessional differences were observed across all topics. Physiotherapists led in falls and mobility (mean 4.21, SD 0.75), pharmacists in polypharmacy and deprescribing (mean 3.51, SD 1.07), and psychologists/psychotherapists in depression (mean 3.96, SD 0.82). A medical doctors–nurses–pharmacists cluster emerged for Knowledge and Interest; 34.4% pharmacists fell in the low relevance class. Social workers and speech and language therapists showed a low Knowledge–high Interest mismatch. EU-27 professionals reported higher scores than non-EU-27 professionals across most topics (P &lt; .001).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Perceived knowledge, relevance and interest showed substantial variation across professions and regions, while revealing shared professional profiles. This may inform team-based interprofessional education.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Profiling perceived knowledge, relevance and interest across geriatric topics of health and social care professionals: multinational electronic cross-sectional survey

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Older adults with non-ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) and cognitive impairment experience higher cardiovascular risk than patients with normal cognition. It remains unclear how cognition should influence whether older adults receive an invasive or conservative treatment strategy.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To compare an invasive and conservative treatment strategy among older adults with NSTEMI and cognitive impairment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study is a pre-specified analysis of the SENIOR-RITA randomised controlled trial. Cognition was measured at randomisation using the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA). Patients were followed up for a median of 4.1 years postrandomisation. The primary outcome was a composite of time to cardiovascular death or nonfatal myocardial infarction (MI).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>MoCA was available for 1455 patients (95.8%) who underwent randomisation. Within the cognitively impaired group (909 patients), the primary outcome occurred in 116 patients (26.8%) in the invasive group and in 141 patients (29.6%) in the conservative group (hazard ratio [HR], 0.85; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.66 to 1.10; P = 0.20). Nonfatal MI occurred in 48 patients (11.1%) in the invasive group and in 75 patients (15.8%) in the conservative group (HR 0.64; 95% CI, 0.44 to 0.92). However, there was no interaction between treatment strategy and cognition.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Among those with evidence of cognitive impairment at randomisation, an invasive treatment strategy did not reduce the primary composite outcome of cardiovascular death or nonfatal MI, and there was no evidence of treatment effect heterogeneity based on cognition. The reduction in nonfatal MI events among those with cognitive impairment should be interpreted as an exploratory finding.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Invasive versus conservative strategy for older patients with myocardial infarction based on cognitive function: the SENIOR-RITA cognition analysis

records.abstract: <jats:p>Introduction: Sarcopenia, an age-related syndrome characterized by progressive loss of muscle mass, decreased muscle strength, and/or reduced physical performance, is associated with disruptions in amino acid and lipid metabolism. This study aimed to investigate serum metabolic alterations associated with sarcopenia in older adults. Methods: In this cross-sectional study, 50 patients with sarcopenia (diagnosed per 2014 AWGS criteria) were matched 1:1 by age and sex with non-sarcopenic controls from a pool of 2,965 individuals. Assessments included skeletal muscle mass, grip strength, and gait speed. Serum metabolomic profiling was conducted using liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS). The screening of differential metabolites: variable importance in the projection (VIP) > 1 derived from the OPLS-DA model, and adjusted p-value based on false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.05 calculated by two-sample t-test. Results: Among 100 participants aged 60–87 years, individuals with sarcopenia showed significantly lower BMI, grip strength, albumin, and ASMI than controls (all p < 0.05), whereas lipid levels were comparable. PCA suggested weak group separation, whereas PLS-DA achieved clearer discrimination by sex and sarcopenia status. Differential metabolites identified in the sarcopenia group included arginine, leucine and histidinyl-histidine, the latter of which exhibited decreased abundance. Concomitant alterations in the levels of lipid metabolites collectively suggest disrupted amino acid and lipid metabolism. Conclusion: Patterns of dysregulated amino acid and fatty acid metabolism were observed in older adults with sarcopenia. Such metabolic disturbances might serve as candidate biomarkers to inform early detection and nutritional intervention strategies.</jats:p>
title: Serum Metabolomic Profiling Reveals Disrupted Amino Acid and Fatty Acid Metabolism in Older Adults with Sarcopenia

records.abstract: <jats:p>Background The heterogeneity within the group of older women challenges balancing overtreatment and undertreatment. The tumor-stroma ratio (TSR) has emerged as a potential prognostic marker. In this study, the prognostic value of the TSR in older women with breast cancer is investigated. Methods Women aged ≥70 years, diagnosed between 2003-2009 with hormone receptor-positive (HR+), human epidermal growth factor 2 (HER2)-negative breast cancer were included, excluding those treated with chemotherapy or neoadjuvant therapy. Results Altogether, 2,974 women were included: 70% had a stroma-low tumor and 30% stroma-high. The likelihood of having a stroma-high tumor increased with age (p = 0.021). Univariable analyses presented worse overall survival (OS; HR 1.106, 95% CI 1.016-1.204, p = 0.020) and unfavorable metastasis-free period (MFP; HR 1.324, 95% CI 1.044-1.680, p = 0.021) in stroma-high patients, but this was not significant in multivariable analyses (OS: p = 0.080, MFP: p = 0.961). In multivariable analyses, the TSR remained prognostic regarding OS in women without relevant comorbidities (HR 1.376, 95% CI 1.144-1.655, p < 0.001), and with a ductal carcinoma and no adjuvant systemic therapy (HR 1.455, 95% CI 1.114-1.900, p = 0.006). Conclusion High stromal content was associated with worse OS and MFP and was especially an independent, unfavorable prognostic factor in patients without relevant comorbidities, and those with a ductal carcinoma and no adjuvant therapy. In these specific patient groups, the TSR could support further personalization of treatment, such as de-escalating therapy in those with favorable prognosis (stroma-low) or by treating those with an unfavorable prognosis (stroma-high) more aggressively.</jats:p>
title: The Prognostic Value of the Tumor-Stroma Ratio (TSR) is Most Pronounced in Older Breast Cancer Patients without Relevant Comorbidities

records.abstract: <jats:p>Introduction: This study aimed to evaluate the dose–response relationship between the Oxidative Balance Score (OBS) and a novel Gompertz law-based biological age (GOLD BioAge) and to quantify the potential mediating contributions of the Systemic Inflammation Response Index (SIRI) and uric acid to high-density lipoprotein cholesterol ratio (UHR). Methods: This cross-sectional study included 20,930 adults aged ≥20 years (weighted mean age: 47.79 years) from seven cycles of the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (2001–2010 and 2015–2018). Survey-weighted regressions were used to estimate independent associations of OBS with GOLD BioAge and Accelerated GOLD BioAge. Restricted cubic spline analysis was performed to assess potential nonlinearity. Robustness was assessed through sensitivity and stratified subgroup analyses. Exploratory mediation analyses using a bootstrap resampling-based framework were performed separately for SIRI and UHR to quantify their potential mediating contributions. Results: The weighted proportion of Accelerated GOLD BioAge in the overall sample was 37.57%. The OBS was inversely and linearly associated with GOLD BioAge (P for nonlinearity = 0.723). In the fully adjusted models, each 1-point increment in OBS was associated with a 0.11-year lower GOLD BioAge (β = −0.11, 95% confidence interval [CI]: −0.13 to −0.10, P < 0.001) and 5% lower odds of Accelerated GOLD BioAge (odds ratio [OR] = 0.95, 95% CI: 0.94 to 0.96, P < 0.001). Compared with the lowest OBS tertile (T1), the highest tertile (T3) had 51% lower odds of Accelerated GOLD BioAge (OR = 0.49, 95% CI: 0.43 to 0.56, P for trend < 0.001). The inverse association was directionally consistent across examined subgroups, although its magnitude differed by sex (P for interaction < 0.001). Exploratory mediation analyses showed that SIRI and UHR accounted for 21.10% and 8.30% of the OBS–GOLD BioAge association, respectively. Conclusions: In a nationally representative sample, higher OBS was linearly associated with lower GOLD BioAge, with SIRI and UHR statistically accounting for part of this association. These findings provide epidemiological evidence that a comprehensive antioxidant-oriented dietary and lifestyle profile is associated with lower biological age, warranting further prospective investigation.</jats:p>
title: Association of the Oxidative Balance Score with GOLD BioAge: Potential Mediating Roles of SIRI and UHR among US Adults

records.abstract: <jats:p>Introduction. While residential greenspace has been linked to better cognitive function in older adults, it remains unclear whether short-term greenspace exposure during everyday mobility can provide immediate cognitive benefits. Stress may play a critical role in this process, as it reflects a mismatch between environmental demands and personal resources and may signal an increased need for restoration. Methods. This ambulatory assessment study examined the association between greenspace exposure and cognition in daily life, as well as the moderating role of stress. Over a two-week period, 123 older adults (aged 65–89 years) wore a GPS device that continuously recorded their mobility trajectories and carried a smartphone to complete repeated working memory tasks and experience sampling assessments of stressors approximately every two hours (seven times per day). Results. Multilevel models showed that, at the within-person level, greater-than-usual greenspace exposure in the past two hours was associated with higher-than-usual momentary working memory performance when stressor occurrence was reported, compared to moments when stressors were not reported. At the between-person level, individuals with higher overall greenspace exposure showed better working memory performance. Conclusions. These findings suggest that the cognitive benefits of greenspace exposure are context-dependent, emerging when stressors were recently present and when the need for restoration may be high. More broadly, our findings point to a dynamic, needs-based process in which everyday mobility through natural environments may support cognitive health among older adults.</jats:p>
title: Greenspace Exposure During Everyday Mobility and Working Memory in Older Adults: Momentary Benefits Amid Stressors
